item.title: Recovering Edward Said’s Voice - Hyperallergic
item.description:
For decades, the word “Palestinian” conjured a very specific image in the minds of many intellectuals and members of the public: the commanding presence of Edward Said, credited with no less than revolutionizing our collective understanding of the dynamics of oppression. Now, as Israel’s genocide in Gaza continues, Said’s legacy is not just urgent, but also, in some spaces, the target of censorship. Today, author Moustafa Bayoumi, who studied under the late critic, activist, and professor at Columbia University, pens a thoughtful review of Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), a new documentary by Maiken Baird whose audio consists almost entirely of Said’s own words. “To recover Said’s voice is to rediscover some of the most compelling arguments that have been made for Palestinian liberation,” Bayoumi writes.

Can contemporary art make us laugh (and not just when we’re making fun of it)? Greta Rainbow visits a New York exhibition that’s all about embracing humor in art, and somewhere between Brian Belott's absurdist fan-embedded assemblages and Ebecho Muslimova’s delightfully transgressive depictions, she learns a thing or two about her own funny bone.

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever

In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die. | Moustafa Bayoumi

item.title: A Tiny Monet With a Wild Backstory Just Fetched More Than 20 Times its Estimate at a Christie’s Day Sale - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The auction houses’ marquee evening sales get all the headlines, with high-eight-figure artworks and high-nine-figure totals, sometimes approaching the billion-dollar mark when the market is flush.

But the more modest daytime sales of lower-priced materials occasionally contain real treasures. When I wrote about them for Artnet News in 2015, experts told me that this is where the houses make a lot of their profits; dealers haunt these sales to stock up on inventory; they are far less stage-managed than the evening events; they may be more indicative of the actual health of the market; and you can find better deals.

And they can occasionally spark serious bidding wars. On Wednesday, a tiny artwork by a titan of French Impressionism became the latest example.

Claude Monet’s La Barque (ca. 1874), which came under the hammer at Christie’s Rockefeller Center saleroom at a day sale of Impressionist and modern art, was estimated at $300,000 to $500,000, but fetched just shy of $7 million. Its modest estimate matched its diminutive size: it measures only 2¾ by 3½ inches, so it sold for $722,285.71 per square inch.

More than 20 bidders fought for the tiny panel, some in the room and some bidding on the phone via Christie’s specialists, says the house; the contest went on for six minutes and 45 seconds, and Rachel White Young, head of the 20th-century evening sale, won the prize for her client.

Even before making a little auction history on Wednesday, the painting had an unusual backstory.

Paris art dealer Georges Petit, a collector and supporter of the Impressionists, commissioned it from the artist; the magazine L’Art Moderne wrote about it in June 1902, relating how the collector carried around small pieces of wood, cut to identical sizes, which he handed out to artists he admired. He would offer them 100 francs and ask if they would return the petite panel as a painting. He did the same with Camille Corot, Édouard Manet, Camille Pissarro, and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, all of whom obliged.

All five would come into the collection of Thérèse and Frédéric Humbert, notorious figures in French high society. She claimed to have been willed a fortune by an imaginary American millionaire, Robert Crawford, whose life she had supposedly saved. They borrowed against an imaginary fortune, buying a grand home and occupying the center of Parisian social life for two decades, until bank officials started asking questions and her creditors sued and the tissue of lies was shredded.

Funny enough, the resulting sale of their possessions would take place in 1902 at none other than Galerie Georges Petit. Galerie Bernheim-Jeune bought it and it remained with that family until 2013, when the ollectors Marlene and Spencer Hays got it at Paris auction house Hôtel Drouot, for the hammer price of €200,000. They began selling books door-to-door as a summer job for Southwestern Company and later went on to run the busines and start a clothing company.

According to their foundation, when asked what was the most fun part of their lives, they would say, “learning about art and building a collection that we treasure,” but would also quote Sir Richard Attenborough to the effect that art collectors are “simply its temporary, fortunate and delighted custodians.” Their collection included works by Pierre Bonnard, Edgar Degas, Henri Matisse, Amedeo Modigliani, and Édouard Vuillard.

They were as good as their word; they granted their collection to Paris’s Musée d’Orsay in 2016. It was the largest foreign collection donated since World War II, with some 600 masterworks from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He died the next year, survived by Marlene.

item.title: Cézanne ‘Arlequin’ Sells for $111 M. at Sotheby’s, Becoming One of the Most Expensive Paintings by the Artist - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Paul Cézanne made his name painting apples and mountains. But on Wednesday night, the artist’s somewhat severe picture of a teenager in costume became one of the most expensive Cézannes ever sold at auction, after selling at Sotheby’s New York for $111 million with fees.

Arlequin (1888–90), a colorful painting of a young man in a red-and-black diamond-patterned costume, hit the block at Sotheby’s during its dedicated evening sale for the Blaquier-Arrieta collection. The painting hammered at $99 million.

It failed to beat the previous record of $137.8 million set by La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888–90), which sold at Christie’s in 2022 as part of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen’s collection. Still, once auctioneer Oliver Barker sold Arlequin tonight, a round of applause followed.

Sotheby’s didn’t publish an estimate for Arlequin prior to the sale, though the painting was expected to bring in around $120 million.

The figure in the painting is Cézanne’s son, Paul, dressed as Harlequin, the mischievous character from Italian commedia dell’arte theater. He wears a pointed hat and an elaborate white collar, and holds a slender baton as he walks across a sharply tilted floor. For someone dressed as a comic character, he looks surprisingly serious.

Cézanne painted the picture in Paris between 1888 and 1890, when he was experimenting with a series of theatrical subjects. There are only four paintings in the group, and Arlequin is the only one still in private hands. The others are in museums, including the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., the Pola Museum of Art in Japan, and the Pushkin Museum in Moscow.

The painting comes with quite a history. It passed through the hands of several of the great dealers of the early modern art market, including Ambroise Vollard and Paul Rosenberg, before become part of Lord Victor Rothschild’s collection during the 1930s. His son, Lord Jacob Rothschild, later inherited it, and in 1975 it was sold through London’s Lefevre Gallery to Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier.

Before leaving for Argentina, the painting appeared in major exhibitions at the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 1929, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1952, and the Tate Gallery in London in 1954. After the Blaquiers bought it, it all but disappeared from public view for half a century.

Sotheby’s had guaranteed the painting before Wednesday’s auction, promising the sellers an undisclosed amount regardless of the outcome. It also secured an irrevocable bid, meaning at least one prospective buyer had committed to bidding before the auction began.

Such arrangements are increasingly common at the top of the art market. According to an analysis by the art-market data firm ARTDAI, just 19 guaranteed Cézanne lots make up 63 percent of the hammer-price value in its database of 640 Cézanne sales. In other words, a small number of exceptionally expensive pictures drive much of the artist’s auction business.

The record-setting Cézanne, La Montagne Sainte-Victoire, hammered at $120 million in 2022, more than twice the price achieved by the artist’s next most expensive auction result, a still life that fetched $60.5 million at Sotheby’s in 1999.

Of course, that auction record doesn’t tell the whole story. A version of Cézanne’s The Card Players was reportedly sold privately to Qatar for around $250 million in 2011, a reminder that some of the biggest deals in the art world never reach a public salesroom.

Arlequin was one of 12 paintings offered from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection on Wednesday, alongside Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), which had been expected to fetch around $180 million and ended up selling for $190.4 million.

item.title: Van Gogh Slashes Auction Record at Sotheby’s, Selling for $190.4 M. - ARTnews.com
item.description:
After a week dominated by a Nazi-era restitution dispute, Sotheby’s finally got to sell a $180 million Vincent van Gogh painting on Wednesday night—for more than it bargained for.

Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), a picture of chestnut trees in bloom painted just weeks before the artist’s death, sold for $190.4 million (including fees), setting a new auction record for the Dutch painter. The painting, which carried an undisclosed guarantee, hammered at $165 million against an expectation of around $180 million (pre-sale estimates do not include buyer’s fees).

After the sale, Kelly Crow reported in the Wall Street Journal that dealer William Acquavella was the painting’s buyer, something that ARTnews also independently confirmed.

The fifth item and cover lot for the Blaquier-Arrieta collection sale, which the house had billed as “legendary,” hung behind the rostrum presided over by auctioneer Oliver Barker.

The artist’s previous record of $117.2 million was set at Christie’s in November 2022 when Verger avec cyprès (1888), a landscape from the collection of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen, sold, hammering for $102 million.

Wednesday’s result beats that by $73.2 million, a jump of 62.4 percent in just four years.

The record is certainly a victory for Sotheby’s, which almost wasn’t going to be able to sell Châtaigniers en fleurs. Last Thursday, descendants of Samuel Fischer, the German Jewish publisher who once owned the painting, challenged its sale, arguing that their family had been forced to part with it in Amsterdam in 1936 because of Nazi persecution. Sotheby’s disputed the claim, pointing to archival records showing the painting had sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, around $22,000 at the time, which it considered a fair market price. After several days of talks, the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the Fischer heirs reached an agreement this week, clearing the painting’s title before the sale. The terms weren’t disclosed, so it’s unclear whether the heirs will receive a share of the proceeds.

For a little perspective, van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr. Gachet (1890) fetched $82.5 million at Christie’s in 1990, then the highest price ever paid for a work of art at auction. That remained the artist’s auction record for 32 years, until the Allen sale. Now, just four years later, the ceiling has moved again.

Painted shortly after van Gogh arrived to Auvers-sur-Oise, Châtaigniers en fleurs is one of only roughly 50 landscapes the artist made during his two-month stay their before his death. Of those, the majority belong to museums, while only an estimated eight are still in private hands, according to research cited by the Art Newspaper.

This electric scene, with its thick brushwork, also hadn’t been seen in decades, last being exhibited at the Guggenheim in 1964. The consignors, Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier, bought it in 1975 and kept it hidden for half a century. That kind of provenance and scarcity is exactly what fuels the trophy market for works of this caliber.

A record of this size for a Post-Impressionist painting might suggest that the market for this category is roaring back. While the market has certainly improved, the rise in sales of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art by 47 percent in 2025 to $1.8 billion, according to the Art Basel and UBS Art Market Report, is still nearly $1 billion short of its $2.6 billion peak in 2022.

item.title: Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Found in NYC Closet Sells for $4.9M - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Welcome to our roundup of daily art news, featuring top stories and timely updates handpicked by Hyperallergic’s writers and editors. Have a news tip? Get in touch with us.

Long-Lost Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Found in Closet Breaks Estimates

Georgia O’Keeffe’s “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” (1930), which was rediscovered in the back of an East Village closet where it was stored for four decades, fetched $4.9 million at Christie’s 20th-Century Evening Sale last night, November 18, surpassing its $2-3 estimate. Read Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar’s report detailing the fascinating backstory behind the painting, created just one year after the artist's first visit to New Mexico.

EU Countries Call to Exclude Russia From Architecture Biennale

Days before the close of this year’s Venice Biennale, 10 European Union countries are demanding that the European Commission exclude Russia from the 2027 architecture biennale. “In light of the current geopolitical realities … there should be no room for ‘normalisation’ of Russia’s participation in international sporting and cultural events, as long as there is no just and lasting peace in Ukraine,” reads a letter signed by representatives in Poland, Austria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden, according to Rapporteur.

Public Art Fund Announces 2027 Program

Ahead of its 50th anniversary next year, Public Art Fund has announced its 2027 exhibition program. The organization will continue its longstanding bus shelter series with I Happen to Like New York, which will transform 700 JCDecaux shelters across New York, Chicago, and Boston with the works of 19 artists, including Nicole Eisenman, Louis Fratino, and Toyin Ojih Odutola. New outdoor public sculptures from Ugo Rondinone, Lotus Kang, and Firelei Báez, a photo series from Catherine Opie, and a first-of-its-kind participatory performance by Jeremy Dweller round out Public Art Fund's 2027 offerings.

More in Today’s News: 

  • Brooklyn artist Julia Jo's "One Fell Swoop" (2026) will be offered at Christie’s evening sale tomorrow, November 19, to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless. The New York-based nonprofit has supported unhoused individuals and families in the city through food, clothing, housing, job training, and youth programs since its founding in 1981. "One Fell Swoop" is estimated to fetch between $30,000 and $50,000, though a Christie’s spokesperson told Hyperallergic that “we think it will go for more.”
  • Two months before the closing of Ana Mendieta at London’s Tate Modern, the Museum of Modern Art has announced it will present the first retrospective on the late Cuban-American artist in the United States in over 20 years.
  • Leading feminist conceptual artist Eleanor Antin has sued her dealer Richard Saltoun, who operates galleries in New York, London, and Rome, over his alleged withholding of at least 179 works.
  • After this month’s “blue wave,” President Donald Trump will soon have to contend with a Democrat-majority Congress ready to investigate his culture war tirades against institutions including the National Portrait Gallery, the Smithsonian, and the Kennedy Center. 
  • This week, the City of Sydney in Australia awarded 40 artists $25,000 “no strings attached” grants in a new initiative aimed at preventing the city from losing “its local storytellers and creative soul.”
  • Five works, including 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and 18th-20th century inscribed crosses, were repatriated to Ethiopia following a ceremony in London today, November 18, as part of a new partnership between the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio and the Ethiopian Heritage Authority.

item.title: Is My Art Funny to You? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare. Called “Duchenne laughter” after a 19th-century neurologist, the gesture is bodily, sometimes to a repulsive degree. But most of the time, we laugh because we feel that we should — that it would behoove us socially. In a talk at the Aspen AIR Festival this year, poet and psychoanalyst Nuar Alsadir described eliciting Duchenne laughter as an attempt “to strip away the layers of socialization and the false self.” While laughter “flies under the radar because of our associations to it as being joyful,” when you dig deeper, it’s “usually coming from some kind of conflict in the unconscious.”

What to make of art that makes us laugh? (Or at least desperately wants to?) Does This Taste Funny?: Humor in Contemporary Art, a sprawling exhibition across at Lehman College Art Gallery in the Bronx and The Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence in Bronxville, proposes comedy as a potent artistic device. Co-curators Melissa Brown, artist and professor of art at Lehman College, and John O’Connor, chair of the Visual and Studio Arts program at Sarah Lawrence, use humor’s various tones — absurd, cringe, slapstick, ironic — as organizing principles to present the work of 41 artists. From museum-collection heavy hitters like Ray Johnson and Cindy Sherman, to established cartoonists Roz Chast and Aline Kominsky-Crumb, to contemporary rising stars such as Ebecho Muslimova, Does This Taste Funny? implores us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.

Humor is “an emotional response that’s a little bit like a sneak attack,” Brown said in an interview with Hyperallergic. “It causes you to think about things in a way that is not led by a press release, not predetermined by art history. There’s something that’s very, very personal about it.” Indeed, humor tends to be anti-didactic. You either guffaw or giggle, or you don’t. Alsadir would say that what you find funny or not provides information about your psychic state — what does it say about me that I chuckled sympathetically at Jill Danenberg’s 2024 accordion book Underground Comic, detailing trials and tribulations between veganism and feminism, while my mouth refused to curl for Tony Matelli’s “Veg Man” (2008), a droopily vegetal bronze figure?

The participatory nature of humor means this show is uniquely invested in perception, and in provoking a certain response. As at an open mic, I felt the pressure of bearing witness, aware of my role as an audience member with the power to deem certain works successful or not by producing that ever-elusive involuntary laugh. This semester, O’Connor is teaching an undergraduate class on taking laughter seriously: He tasked his students with making small sculptures, their only instruction to try to be “the funniest in the class.” The winning piece, according to votes cast via smiley-face stickers on a table outside the gallery, is a realistic bust of Professor O’Connor with a No. 2 pencil stuck halfway up his nose. Second place was a reference to a meme O’Connor still doesn’t quite understand.

The oldest featured work in Does This Taste Funny? is Karl Wirsum’s drawing “Untitled (Study for Blue Tattoo)” (1964), featuring a classic Sailor Jerry star design on the tongue of a woman sporting a perfect mid-century housewife hairdo. Getting the reference is important to appreciating a good joke beyond the most base level of someone farting or slipping on a banana peel (which, to get psychoanalytic again, we laugh at to mask our own shame). Brown and O’Connor’s curation is never insidery or niche to the canon, but they are aware of the quality of funniness changing over time.

Some of O’Connor’s students recognized River Phoenix in Ray Johnson’s mail-art collage; more were taken by Jeremy Couillard’s “Escape from Lavender Island” (2023), an open-world video game simulation featuring deep-fried animation aesthetics and relatably tragic dialogue from the depths of neoliberal hell (“While he ate he would watch film classics on an overpriced streaming service and sometimes cry.”) 

“Absurdism ends up being pretty timeless,” Brown said. “Using ridiculously absurd materials to make work that doesn’t connect necessarily to a political moment or a socioeconomic issue, it represents this irreverent attitude towards art-making.” And apparently that’s what appeals to Gen Z, who are inundated with visual content, yet perhaps still seeking a response to contemporary life that truly resonates. 

Brown, who has been teaching at Lehman for 20 years, wants artists to find their idiosyncratic voice. If being funny comes naturally, maybe that’s the tack they should take.

“There’s such a tendency for imitation out there. You can easily become a version of something that exists, and that is no longer considered a bad thing,” she said. “I'm interested in trying to find, ‘What's your really weird way of approaching that?’”

Take Kristen Mills’s “It IS Cake” (2026), a filmic parody of the Netflix baking contest series Is It Cake? using entirely brown cardboard, displayed in the gallery on a screen within a faux kitchen made of the same plainly bland material. Installed nearby is puppet theater ephemera that does directly respond to a political moment: John Vasquez Mejias’s “The Puerto Rican War” (2026), which expands his novelette about revolutionaries fighting colonialism in 1950. The Puerto Ricans’ demands aren’t funny, but some of the depictions of American incompetence are.

Does This Taste Funny? reminds us of humor as a tool, as a way to frame whatever it is that we hope to communicate. Life is not always joyful, but it should at least be emotional. At Sarah Lawrence, I watched Robert DeJesus’s surreal video “The Survey” (2024), starring a talking Olmec head who speaks only when there are no corroborative witnesses. I didn’t laugh. Later in the day, turning a corner on the grounds of Lehman College, I was suddenly confronted with the stone statue, whose onscreen lips I’d just seen move. I audibly snorted.

item.title: Phillips Evening Sale Tops $104 M., Led By $44.6 M. Modigliani Sculpture - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Phillips’s modern and contemporary evening sale, held at its Park Avenue headquarters in New York on Tuesday night, garnered $104.4 million with fees on 22 lots, led by a $44.6 million total for the 1911–12 Amedeo Modigliani sculpture Tête.

With one lot withdrawn prior to sale and only one lot going unsold, the sale posted a healthy 95 percent sell-through rate by lot and an even more impressive 99 percent sell-through rate by value.

In a post-sale email, the auction house, which has recently faced scrutiny following cost-cutting and a major leadership shake-up in August, touted the total as a 55 percent increase over the equivalent sale last year. That figure is correct, but it does not tell the whole story. The 2025 edition of the modern and contemporary evening sale generated $67.3 million on 33 lots with two unsold. This year’s edition was pulled up considerably by the Modigliani result. Remove that from the total and the take drops to $59.8 million, though that is spread across 20 lots rather than 31. Still impressive, all things considered, but not quite the mega-result the house is touting.

But credit where credit is due: Phillips specialists did secure that Modigliani consignment, and it significantly outperformed its $28–$35 million estimate. Other strong results for the night were the eight-panel David Hockney group portrait David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982, which landed within its $10–$15 million presale estimate for a total of $12.2 million with fees; the Alexander Calder sculpture Snow Flurry, May 14 (1959), which reached $7.5 million with fees on a $4–$6 million estimate; and the Helen Frankenthaler landscape Seabreeze (1980), which sold for $4.5 million with fees, well above its $2.5 million high estimate.

Phillips noted that the Hockney is the artist’s highest result at auction this year. Three other Hockney paintings appeared at Christie’s and Sotheby’s this week, the highest selling for $8.05 million at Sotheby’s contemporary evening sale on Monday, per ARTDAI.

In the same email, Robert Manley, chairman and global head of modern and contemporary art, said the sale’s strongest results were due to offering “fresh-to-market, museum-quality material.” He added, “Tonight’s results are a powerful reminder that truly exceptional works continue to inspire extraordinary competition in the market.”

That takeaway aligns with the results of the week’s other major sales so far: Sotheby’s The Now and contemporary evening sales on Monday and Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on Tuesday. At both houses, there was strong, deep bidding for truly exceptional works, but also more than a few unsold lots and spotty interest in those that didn’t reach that A+ level.

As art advisor Ralph De Luca put it succinctly to ARTnews during Tuesday’s sale at Christie’s, “The flight to quality is astounding.” Indeed.

item.title: Arpita Singh, Indian Painter Who Never Stopped Innovating, Dies at 89 - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In Memoriam honors those we recently lost in the art world.

Arpita Singh (1937–2026)
Indian painter who bridged fantasy and reality

One of the most high-profile contemporary Indian artists, Singh fused violent realism and fantasy imagery, constantly innovating across a six-decade career. In the 1970s and '80s, for instance, she explored abstraction, producing spare compositions filled with dots and dashes. She became more widely known in the West due to an exhibition at Serpentine Galleries just last year.

"Singh never settles into a mode or style," critic John Yau wrote in a 2017 review of her exhibition at New Delhi- and New York-based Talwar Gallery for this magazine. "This body of work, which is being shown for the first time in America, is a singular achievement."

item.title: MoMA to Host First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Over 20 Years - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The indelible impact of late Cuban-American artist Ana Mendieta's practice will be celebrated in a forthcoming retrospective in New York next year. Scheduled to open at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in Manhattan in December 2027, Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective marks the first presentation of Mendieta's overarching career in the United States in over 20 years.

MoMA's announcement comes just two months before Tate Modern's ongoing Mendieta retrospective closes in London. Comprising around 200 works, including rarely seen formative drawings and newly remastered films, the MoMA exhibition will present Mendieta's artistic process, signature developments, and career milestones in a chronological fashion. Starting with early figurative works completed during her undergraduate and graduate studies at the University of Iowa, the exhibition will follow the artist's subsequent expansion in making and documenting her performance art, as well as her foray into sculpture, installation, and site-specific land art.

Born in Cuba and raised in Iowa from age 12 as a child evacuee through Operation Peter Pan, Mendieta ruminated on themes of displacement, ancestral memory, ecology, and the politics of the female body, as well as its connection with the natural world. She's best known for her Silueta (1973–80) series, in which the outline of her body (either present or absent) is embedded, extruded, burned, or embellished into various natural environments as a physical and spiritual reunion with the earth. These “earth-body works,” as Mendieta called them, dealt with Mesoamerican and Afro-Caribbean divinity, natural reclamation and life cycles, and the deconstruction of borders.

Presaging Mendieta's groundbreaking Siluetas were transgressive performance pieces centering the use of blood as a signifier of violence, fertility, vitality, and ancestral ritual. Her 1973 performance “Untitled (Rape Scene)” and its photo documentation were created in response to the rape and murder of 20-year-old University of Iowa student Sarah Ann Ottens, whereas her filmed performance of “Untitled (Death of a Chicken)” (1972) graphically referenced animal sacrifice practices associated with Santería.

The retrospective also centers the artist's lens-based work, her sustained interest in organic material, and how her travels, reunion with Cuba, and art residencies sparked major evolutions in her practice. Mendieta's 1981 Esculturas Rupestres (Rupestrian Sculptures) series, 1983–85 fellowship at the American Academy in Rome, and a variety of later works, including a series of ink-wash drawings, are among the highlights mentioned by the museum.

“Ana Mendieta rigorously investigated the physical, conceptual, and emotional potential of materials like soil, sand, water, blood, leaves, wood, and fire to create images that speak across time and geography,” said Beverly Adams, MoMA's Latin American art curator and retrospective co-organizer, in a press statement. “In doing so, she redefined the boundaries between sculpture and action, object and image, and private and public.”

In celebrating Mendieta's punctuated career, the retrospective apparently strays away from the tragic circumstances of the 36-year-old artist's death and the unshakeable speculations that continue to follow. Such is the case with Mendieta's ongoing exhibition at the Tate Modern, which also omitted mentioning the artist's death and the resulting controversy surrounding her husband, artist Carl Andre.

Nevertheless, the artist's own poignant grapplings with loss and rebirth are staged independently of the discourse, underscoring her persisting critical impact in a visual arts landscape that has rarely offered credit to women artists.

Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective will be on view at MoMA from December 12, 2027 to April 15, 2028.

item.title: Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die.  

While Salloum and Suleiman’s film consists mostly of news clips and film reels, one of Gaza’s elder statesmen, the late Haider Abdul Shafi, does appear briefly twice. In one scene, Abdul Shafi, sitting at a nondescript table, is asked by an interviewer: “Is it your belief that if a Palestinian state was created, there would be lasting peace in the Middle East?” Just as he’s about to respond, the film mischievously cuts away, in an edit loaded with meaning. Palestinians may be seen in Western media, the film is telling us, but they cannot be heard from.

Maiken Baird’s new documentary, Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), joyfully demonstrates how Edward Said was the exception to this semi-official ban on Palestinians representing themselves. Like Salloum and Suleiman, Baird also sifts through reservoirs of found footage, though the result couldn’t be more different. Offering a rough chronology of Said’s life, Baird’s film celebrates him by highlighting his contributions and lasting influence in numerous domains, from literary theory to American foreign policy. 

For decades, the Columbia University professor of comparative literature was the most famous, if not the only, Palestinian regularly speaking on American airwaves and writing about the Palestinians in its magazines. Wearing his bespoke suits and contributing classical music criticism to the Nation, Said cut an urbane, sophisticated, and cosmopolitan figure. 

But it was his substance, and not his style, that earned him his legacy. As the author of the foundational text Orientalism, Said was one of the most influential intellectuals of the 20th century, and he took the vocation extremely seriously, holding the yes-men intellectuals of the powerful in contempt. As he wrote in his essay “Secular Criticism": “It is not practicing criticism to validate the status quo.” For Said, an intellectual must always oppose domination while cultivating resistance to oppression. 

I am one of the fortunate ones. I knew Edward Said personally, having studied under him while I completed my PhD at Columbia University. With Andrew Rubin, another of his students, I edited The Selected Works of Edward Said: 1996-2006 (2019). (A producer of this film contacted me during its early phase for a background discussion on Said and his life, but I had nothing to do with the making of this documentary.) It’s hard to believe that more than 20 years have passed since Said died from leukemia in 2003, but thanks to Baird’s documentary, a new generation can now access his indomitable energy and inexhaustible fight for justice. 

With the question of Palestine currently assuming a new urgency around the world, and with Israel’s genocide of Gazans ongoing, the timing of the film feels like a deliberate intervention. To recover Said’s voice is to rediscover some of the most compelling arguments that have been made for Palestinian liberation. It’s no mistake that, aside from hearing a few interviewers’ questions and small asides, the audio of this 108-minute film consists almost entirely of Said speaking.

Produced with the cooperation of the Said family, the film includes moments from early home movies taken by Wadie Said, Edward Said’s father. The elder Said purchased a movie camera in 1938 and made “incredibly boring” films, according to the younger. By including snippets of these early scenes, Baird does something more than show us a young and gangly Edward Said. The home movies not only invite viewers into the private life of a Palestinian family in Palestine. They also become an assertion of presence against an ideology which demands Palestinian absence.

Young Edward was entirely apolitical. As a teenager, he was expelled for being a “troublemaker” from Victoria College in Egypt and sent by his family to the “puritanical” Mount Hermon School in rural Massachusetts, where, as he says, he was mocked endlessly for his name (“Ed Said. Well, what did he say?”). An elite education at Princeton and Harvard followed, and then a job as an assistant professor at Columbia University. “The professional thing took care of itself,” he says. But after the humiliating Arab defeats of the 1967 war, Said felt a need to reconcile the two parts of himself: an American professor of literature and a Palestinian Arab born in Jerusalem. In the wake of the losses in 1967, his friend Ibrahim Abu-Lughod invited him to contribute an essay to the United States-based magazine The Arab World, and Said wrote “The Arab Portrayed,” his first significant foray into the politics of representation. 

In the film, Said describes his decisions to take on the Palestinian cause, and his father’s caution to his son: “I’m very worried about what the Zionists will do to you." In the early 1970s, while living in Beirut, he immerses himself in the Arabic language and literature and associates with some of the preeminent Palestinian intellectuals of the era. The film’s tempo picks up as Said’s star begins to shine more brightly. We watch him being asked borderline racist questions in multiple TV interviews, see him with Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) leader Yasser Arafat, and despair with him when the Israeli invasion of Lebanon leads to the expulsion of the PLO from Lebanon in 1982. 

Said was the most prominent dissenting Palestinian voice to the 1993 Oslo Accords. He believed the PLO had sold out the Palestinian national movement, only to become “Israel’s enforcer” of the occupation. Baird’s film successfully shows how he went from being a fierce critic of American and Israeli policy to a fierce critic of American, Israeli, and Palestinian leadership. I knew Said at this time in his life, and what the film doesn’t show is the profound sense of isolation he felt while the entire global liberal establishment was telling us that “the conflict,” as it’s euphemistically called, was about to be solved. Needless to say, Said was right.

Music was a grounding force in Said’s life (he was a near-concert-level pianist) and another constant in the film. Baird ends her film with his growing friendship with the Argentinian-Israeli composer Daniel Barenboim. Said and Barenboim began the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra, a musical venture bringing together young Arab and Israeli musicians, in 1999, the same year his essay “The One-State Solution” was published in the New York Times. The essay argued that “real peace can come only with a binational Israeli-Palestinian state.” 

In the final years of his life, Said committed himself to such efforts at coexistence. The last scene of this finely tuned documentary is of him playing the piano with passionate intensity. “It’s not our destiny to be refugees," he says via voiceover. "It’s not our destiny to be prisoners of war. It’s not our destiny to be commandos. It’s not our destiny to be an army of occupation. We have a choice.” 

There is more than a whiff of optimism in these later positions, and it’s impossible to say where Said would stand today, as Palestinians face their most demanding fight for survival yet. But the fact that his optimism feels somewhat dated today probably tells us less about Said and more about how far away we are now from attaining true and lasting justice for the Palestinians.

Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), directed by Maiken Baird, is screening at various film festivals including the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam, London Palestine Film Festival, Marrakech International Film Festival, and many more. It will be released widely in 2027 by Kino Lorber.

item.title: Nina Kintsurashvili's Paintings of Yearning - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Copious research materials drawn from her country’s rich and complex history are integral to Georgian painter Nina Kintsurashvili. She doesn’t depict them — including ancient frescoes, Byzantine icons, earthenware vessels, books, or Soviet-era illustrations — but instead obliquely alludes to, channels, and transforms them in largely abstract yet partially figural paintings. 

Her new paintings (all oil on linen from 2026) are luscious yet willfully scruffy, with paint often applied thickly and sometimes erased, and with brushstrokes ranging from vigorous and broad to wispy and spindly. In “Rifts,” creamy, sinewy, irregularly shaped forms spread horizontally from border to border. Underneath, multicolored vertical bands pull the picture plane downward, as if under gravity. There is motion here — pressure, tension — a shifting terrain. At the very bottom is something curious, which crops up often in these works: a grid, or rather a snippet of a grid. It could be the magnified warp and weft of the linen. It could be a section of fence.

item.title: Hand-Marbled Papers Ground Sylvain Lefebvre’s Surreal Landscapes - Colossal
item.description:
Enormous trees dominate dreamlike wooded landscapes in the mixed-media paintings of Sylvain Lefebvre. A spectral form with dense, gnarly branches shelters a lounging woman in “The Quercus Corallium,” and a table alive with conversation nests beneath the canopy in “A Debat at Tea Time.”

The French artist’s Journeys Into the Unseen Forest at Rebecca Hossack Art Gallery comprises a series of almost fairytale-like tableaux. Collaged, hand-marbled papers beneath the delicate layers of oil paint represent the barely visible or unknown. And trees group closely in the background darken in the distance, while diminutive figures climb around and relax at the base of monumental trunks.

Summer 2026 marked France’s hottest ever documented since records began, during which rainfall was low and unprecedented wildfires raged. Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, where the effects of the climate crisis are dramatic and impossible to ignore. In Journeys Into the Unseen Forest, Lefebvre delves into an imaginary realm where humans coexist harmoniously with flora and fauna, and old-growth sentinels harbor a wide range of life.

The artist says, “I wanted to put myself in the place of a forest and its trees by asking myself the following question: How is it that when we look at nature, whatever form it takes, it always appears balanced, while the trees that make it up can grow in such unbalanced ways… twisted, diagonally or horizontally, struggling to find their way towards the light?”

In “The Quercus Corallium,” a white tree glows like a sacred spirit, and in “The Polyphane Pachidermus,” one can imagine the canopy extending forever into the blue distance. “In the unseen forest, [Lefebvre] discovers species of trees that have never been seen before,” the gallery says. “They are completely plausible species that may exist somewhere in the few corners of the world that have not yet been discovered. Perhaps they are trees of the future.”

Journey Into the Unseen Forest continues through December 23 in London. See more on Lefebvre’s Instagram.

item.title: New York City’s Transit System Has the State’s Greatest ‘Underground Museum.’ Here’s Why It’s Worth Visiting. - ARTnews.com
item.description:
New York has the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum, the Frick Collection, and countless other great art institutions. Yet one of the city’s most well-rounded ones is an “underground museum” that can be found largely in the subway, with certain pieces also visible at Metro-North and Long Island Rail Road train stops.

That was the terminology used by Tina Vaz, director of the MTA’s Arts & Design program, in a talk held this past Friday at the PMC Studio as part of Art Week NYC, a festival of programming put on across the city by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America.

“This is a dynamic transit environment, but even in all of the noise and movement and motion, the works get through and people connect with them,” Vaz said. She cited a survey in which 80 percent of respondents said they noticed the artworks at MTA, Metro-North, and LIRR stops, which have been done by artists ranging from William Wegman to Yayoi Kusama. That people were aware of these works, Vaz said, is “double proof of concept.”

Vaz’s latest commissions are by artists Ivan Forde, Trevor Paglen, and Howardena Pindell, who are respectively in the process of making new works for the Broadway Junction subway stop and the Metro-North’s Southeast and Botanical Garden stops. Forde and Pindell joined Vaz on Friday to discuss their commissions.

Forde’s, a mosaic called Bedtime Story for Brownsville: The Fish Who Carried the Moon (2026), grew out of his sketches and poetry. In his mosaic, the Moon is what he called a “main character.” “The Moon has lost her way, and she fell into the sea,” he said. “These fish, they come and they help her, and they guide her back to the sky … It’s really thinking about structures of epic poetry.”

Pindell is making a glass installation based on photographs she took over the course of a day at the New York Botanical Garden. “Once they were developed, I cut them into sections and laid them out along part of the station wall,” she said. “Then, there were arrows put in.” Through the installation, “you are seeing the inside of the garden, both the domed building as well as along the paths.”

item.title: How “American Gothic” Took On a Life of Its Own - Hyperallergic
item.description:
You already know the image by heart: Two stern figures stand before an old wooden house. To the left, a blonde, blue-eyed woman wears an apron and a somber expression. Beside her, an unsmiling man in glasses and overalls grips a pitchfork. Since it was first exhibited at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1930, Grant Wood’s painting has joined the ranks of art historical touchstones and shown up in countless ads, books, and memes. But what made this unassuming image so popular, and why does it continue to captivate us today?

In The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon (2026), art historian and curator Wanda M. Corn provides some compelling answers. The author began writing about Wood’s painting in 1981, and she has spent decades amassing an archive of “American Gothic”-related imagery that tracks the farm couple across General Mills cereal ads, Gordon Parks’s 1942 portrait of African-American janitor Ella Watson during his fellowship with the Farm Security Administration, magazine covers, COVID-era cartoons, and other surprising riffs. Her book traces the painting’s history from the controversy behind its creation and the bitter fallout it brought to its hapless maker through to its transformation into a pop culture cornerstone and a symbol of Wood’s home state.

item.title: Vhils and Marcelo Cidade Cloak a São Paulo Colonial Building in Silver Thermal Blankets - Colossal
item.description:
“A construction can remain standing while losing its place in the everyday experience of the city. Its address remains, but its presence no longer draws attention. In this sense, disappearance can begin before demolition,” says a statement about a recent collaboration between Alexandre Farto (a.k.a. Vhils) and Marcelo Cidade.

The monumental project at Rua Cardeal Arcoverde, 2878 in Pinheiros, São Paulo, is a meditation on this sentiment as it considers how architecture and the seemingly mundane fixtures of city life shape our understanding of a place. Titled “2878,” the site-specific installation envelops a colonial-style building in silver thermal blankets typically used in emergencies. A cornstarch glue binds the utilitarian material to the structure’s facade, revealing the arched windows and ornate patterns in relief.

Both drawing attention to the building and masking its real condition, the metallic blankets prompt questions about how we care for places and spaces. As passersby walk past, the installation mirrors their silhouettes as faint reflections, while the surface’s color and light shift depending on the time of day.

The collaborative intervention also evokes Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s “Wrapped Reichstag” and the early years of Andy Warhol’s Factory, in which silver paint and tin foil covered the walls of the artist’s New York studio. Warhol was interested in transience and the attention that comes with fame, concerns we see echoed and translated into broader conversations about public space, collective memory, and urban life in “2878.”

Find more from Vhils and Cidade on their Instagrams.

item.title: Meticulously Detailed Animal Portraits by Thomas Cian Pop from the Page - Colossal
item.description:
As if ready to swim right off of the page, Thomas Cian’s fish and other creatures are rendered in exquisite detail. Known for his realistic black-and-white portraits, the artist recently embarked on a series of hyperrealistic animal drawings in gouache and pencil. The new direction took him somewhat by surprise, as he realized one day he had been focusing much more on fauna than he had in years past.

“I think it has a lot to do with a desire to reconnect with everything that exists independently of human beings,” Cian tells Colossal. He felt compelled to get closer to what he describes as elemental raw matter, generated through eons of mysterious and fascinating evolutionary processes. “I think that’s what it comes down to: drawing something that hasn’t itself been designed by someone else.”

Cian’s technical aptitude is obvious, but for him, a work isn’t truly complete unless there’s another kind of investment. “For me, achieving a result I’m truly satisfied with is a considerable challenge because my approach is emotional long before it is descriptive,” he says. Truly understanding and sympathizing with a creature propels the process.

Light also plays an integral role in his deceptively simple monochrome approach: Cian highlights whatever the light touches and leaves everything else alone. A piece feels finished when “areas that remain black stop feeling black,” he says, balancing perception and technicality in equal measure.

The artist spends hours researching a subject before rendering it on paper, watching documentaries and browsing publications that give him a sense of their habitats and behaviors, but he resists working from printed images. Even the textures that, from a distance, may look realistic, are actually intuitive and imagined. “I never copy photographs,” Cian says. “I study the anatomy and then reconstruct it, sometimes exaggerating certain features, in a pose that allows me to feel as though I’m in the presence of that particular creature.”

See more on the artist’s Instagram.

item.title: Eleanor Antin Sues Dealer for Withholding Nearly 200 Works - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Conceptual artist Eleanor Antin is seeking the return of at least 179 works or $975,000 in compensatory damages in a lawsuit against her dealer, Richard Saltoun. The complaint was filed in New York State Supreme Court on July 29, six months after the artist terminated her relationship with Saltoun’s namesake gallery, which operates locations in New York, London, and Rome.

Filed by the 91-year-old artist’s son and attorney-in-fact, Blaise Antin, and her studio, Paranoid Productions, the suit claims that Saltoun “initially purported to agree to return all of the works it held” upon their business separation at the gallery's London location on January 16. News of the lawsuit was first reported by Artnet.

Saltoun claimed in February that the gallery had returned all of Antin’s works to her family, according to filed documents. However, later that month, the artist’s archivist, citing an inventory produced by Saltoun himself, allegedly discovered that Antin was still missing at least 179 works, the majority of which were still held at the London gallery.

item.title: Anti-Monuments to Trump - Hyperallergic
item.description:
When Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, I was in the last place I wanted to be: Washington, DC. Where would I go? I wanted nothing to do with his administration’s empty grandeur. I spent the day at Maya Lin’s Vietnam War Memorial, a dark wound in the earth. In this much more hopeful moment post-midterms, Ed Simon asks a related question: How should memorials remember the MAGA era? He points to historical anti-fascist examples in Germany — and also suggests the bulldozing of Trump’s ballroom to rubble as its own kind of monument. 

Satire’s not a bad strategy to record this era, either. Also today, Greg Werkheiser pens an obituary for the National Historic Preservation Act. The act’s next of kin, the National Register of Historic Places, he writes, “is said to be concerned about its own health.”

Finally, don’t miss the newest installation of Jennifer Samet’s “Beer With a Painter” column. She interviews Ivorian painter Ouattara Watts, who works only at night, when the veil between this world and the next is thinnest. Plus, The Met and the Shanghai Museum are teaming up, just weeks after MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Museum joined forces. They say art imitates life; I just didn’t know that meant we were getting museum oligopolies.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?

Anti-monumentalism responds not with grand equestrian statues or neoclassical columns, but with absence and anxiety, minimalism and melancholy. | Ed Simon
