item.title: Kennedy Family Joins Litigation Opposing Trump’s Triumphal Arch - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The opposition to President Trump’s 250-foot triumphal arch has gained a formidable ally: the Kennedy family.

Nine members of the Kennedy family moved on Tuesday to join ongoing litigation in Washington, D.C., seeking to halt the project before construction begins. Echoing a central criticism of the project, the Kennedys argue that the arch would cast a shadow over the graves of their relatives buried at Arlington National Cemetery. The filing adds that the structure would obstruct the solemn sightline from the eternal flame at President John F. Kennedy’s gravesite, across Memorial Bridge to the Lincoln Memorial, “destroying an essential element of the gravesite’s design.”

Two of the plaintiffs, Rory and Maxwell Kennedy, children of Robert F. and Ethel Kennedy, said in a statement to the New York Times: “A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come.”

Since its unveiling last year, the president’s pet project has advanced in fits and starts. The Trump administration has pushed it past major hurdles, only to see federal courts repeatedly impose temporary blocks. The arch, whose various proposed designs have featured a flame, gilded angels, and a sniper’s nest, received final approval last Thursday from a commission allied with Trump. Only hours later, however, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day restraining order, accompanied by a 33-page opinion that that revisited several of the project’s chief legal and practical challenges: whether it required congressional approval, the costs it would impose on Virginia and the District of Columbia, and the potential disruption to traffic around the heavily traveled Memorial Circle.

The Kennedys, in their suit, reiterated the point: “Only Congress has the constitutional power to authorize an intrusion of this magnitude. Today, members of the Kennedy family are joining with the other litigants in this case to protect this historic site — and to defend the rule of law and separation of powers.”

Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, told the Times that it was “unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the arch, as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery.”

He continued: “The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation. We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds.”

item.title: German Art Historian Reattributes Renoir Print Previously Believed to Be a Fake - ARTnews.com
item.description:
German art historian Henry Keazor has reattributed a work on paper to Pierre-Auguste Renoir that had previously been labeled a forgery.

Keazor is the founder of the Heidelberg Forgery Study Collection (HeFäStuS), which is “a collaboration with the three state criminal investigation offices of Berlin, Bavaria, and Baden-Württemberg, which provide forgeries from their evidence rooms as loans for research and teaching purposes,” according to its website. Students at the University of Heidelberg, where Keazor is a professor of modern and contemporary art history, have first-hand access to its 140 forgeries of artists like Vincent van Gogh, Salvador Dalí, and Alberto Giacometti, so they can “can become aware of the phenomenon of art forgery and learn how to recognize it,” according to its website.

In 2023, a private collector decided to offer the drawing to Keazor and the HeFäStuS as part of a “household clearance”; the owner had inherited the work in the 1970s from a friend who ran a New York gallery that “classed [the work] as a fake,” per a release. The gallery had also given the medium for the work as a pencil drawing.

“While unpacking it I noticed immediately that it was a print, not an original pencil drawing,” Keazor said in a statement. That led him and his students to begin conducting research into Renoir’s works on paper and subjecting the piece to paper and microscopic analyses, which revealed that the “the structure of the autotype paper” and confirmed that “signature is written by hand with black grease chalk,” according to Keazor.

They now believe that it is hand-signed lithograph, dating to around 1899 and depicting actor and singer Amelie Diéterle. The work matches one that Renoir produced for “Germinal,” an artist portfolio that also included works by Degas, van Gogh, and Toulouse-Lautrec.

Keazor now believes that the HeFäStuS print was a test for the portfolio works, which were produced in an edition of 100 and have their signatures printed on the work as opposed to handwritten. “The solution to the riddle is that the picture is a test print made with only one of the two print stones. Since the signature evidently lay on another stone, Renoir added it by hand, thereby making the proof a fully valid work,” Keazor said, noting that such test prints are rare in art history.

The work will go on view at the Kurpfälzisches Museum in Heidelberg from November 26 to March 21 as part of an exhibition titled “Riddle around Renoir.” Afterward, the HeFäStuS and the previous owner will decide “where to keep the print in future,” per a release.

item.title: Betsy James Wyeth’s Placemaking Prowess - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The woman portrayed in Andrew Wyeth’s “Christina’s World” (1948), Christina Olson, has become one of the most iconic figures in American art. Less familiar, perhaps, is the woman who also posed for this painting: his wife, Betsy James Wyeth. Dubbed the “chief architect of the Wyeth mystique,” Betsy shaped the Wyeth brand, Andrew’s life, and art for over seven decades in undeniable ways. Though she rarely occupied the spotlight herself, her influence was everywhere: she handled his business affairs, controlled his public image, wrote books about his art, and maintained his catalogue raisonné. She also served as a creative advisor, critiquing his paintings and giving them their titles.

By Design: The Worlds of Betsy James Wyeth — a hefty and compelling new book (Rizzoli Electa) and a sprawling trio of linked exhibitions shown simultaneously at the Farnsworth Art Museum in Rockland, Maine; Brandywine Museum of Art in Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania; and Colby College Museum of Art in Waterville, Maine — pay tribute to the pair’s enduring partnership and work to credit Betsy as a key figure in her own right.

item.title: Trisha Baga, Laylah Ali, and Kay WalkingStick Among Anonymous Was A Woman Awardees - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Anonymous Was A Woman (AWAW), a nonprofit supporting women, trans, and non-binary artists above 40, named 15 artists working across various media in the United States to receive unrestricted $50,000 awards in recognition of their practices.

AWAW has been doling out awards since it was founded by artist Susan Unterberg in 1996 in response to the National Endowment for the Arts' decision to terminate individual-based grants. Recognizing the unattributed and undersung creative output of women artists, Unterberg named the program after a line from Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own (1929): “I would venture to guess that Anon, who wrote so many poems without signing them, was often a woman.”

The 2026 awardees include artists Laylah Ali, Marsha Pels, Beatriz Cortez, and Katherine Sherwood. Cherokee Nation painter Kay WalkingStick is the eldest recipient at 91 years old, whereas New York City-based video and installation artist Trisha Baga, 41, just made the program's cutoff.

item.title: The Elie Khouri Art Foundation Appoints Sumayya Vally of Counterspace as Architect to Design the Foundation - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Elie Khouri, the French-Lebanese philanthropist and entrepreneur, who is readying his contemporary art foundation, the Elie Khouri Art Foundation (Ekaf), to open in 2028 in Dubai, has appointed architect Sumayya Vally of Counterspace to design the foundation. This year, Khouri appeared on ARTnews’s Top 200 Collectors list.

The foundation will house its own permanent collection. Although, Khouri’s art collection features paintings by Julie Curtiss and Gunther Förg along with pieces by Carol Bove, Dana Schutz, Kehinde Wiley, and more. He started collecting in the late 2000s by acquiring a work by the Lebanese painter Nabil Nahas. Since then, he has been adding 30 to 35 works every year to his collection. Khouri also sits on Tate’s Middle East and North Africa Acquisitions Committee and the Museum of Modern Art’s Media and Performance Committee.

“Art belongs in everyday life, not apart from it. My foundation will be a home for contemporary art, open to everyone,” said Khouri in a statement. “A place to inspire, challenge and spark dialogue. Above all, I want to give something lasting back to Dubai and the wider UAE, a country that has given me so much, by helping build a cultural legacy for generations to come.”

Ekaf will be located in Jumeirah 1, where Vally will be transforming an existing villa into a home for the foundation with galleries, pavilions and a garden, as well as hospitality and outdoor spaces.

“I think of buildings as having many lives. At EKAF, we begin with a house that has already held a world within it. Its doors, cornices, balustrades, and particular ways of receiving people and separating rooms contain the traces of another life,” said Vally in a statement.

The South African architect designed the 20th Serpentine Pavilion in 2021, making her the youngest to do so.

In January 2026, the foundation named art consultant Caroline Louca as its director; Louca previously held the position of managing director of Christie’s Middle East. Louca moved to the United Arab Emirates in 2008, helping the Abu Dhabi Tourism and Culture Authority build its network of museums, including the Louvre Abu Dhabi, Guggenheim Abu Dhabi and the Zayed National Museum.

“A building shapes what people do with art before a single work is hung. Our ambition is for EKAF to be a place where art is not only shown but properly looked at, questioned and talked about,” said Louca in a statement. “Architecture has a big part to play in that: how you arrive, how you move from one room to the next, whether you end up in conversation with a stranger. Counterspace treats a building as a place people use, not an object to admire, and that is the instinct we wanted.”

item.title: Ted Turner’s Western Art Collection to Sell at Christie’s for $20 M. - ARTnews.com
item.description:
With Western art rising as an ascendant category on the auction block, Christie’s is selling works from the collection of Ted Turner, the media mogul who died earlier this year at 87.

According to CNN, the works are valued at around $20 million. That means the results for Turner’s works are unlikely to near the ones Christie’s achieved earlier this year when it sold a tranche of art about the American West from the holdings of William Koch, who will also part with works by Claude Monet and Paul Cézanne this November.

And yet, the Turner collection could prove an unlikely hit, if the Koch sale is any proof. Pegged at $50 million ahead of the sale, the Koch works ended up selling in January for more than $84 million once premiums fees were counted in. According to Christie’s, the Koch sale now holds the record for a single-owner sale of American Western art.

The Turner sale is set to be headlined by an Alfred Bierstadt landscape that long hung above a fireplace in the businessman’s Montana ranch. Titled Yosemite Valley (1866), the painting depicts a placid vision of a tree-lined lake under a blue sky. There are no people here, suggesting that the land was untouched and free for the taking, even though Native Americans resided here.

Turner bought the painting at Sotheby’s in 2003, when the work was given a $6 million high estimate. It was at the time considered one of the most significant Bierstadt works to head to auction in two decades. This time around, the work once again has a $6 million high estimate. Bierstadt’s current auction record, set in 2008, stands at $7.3 million.

Also coming to auction from the Turner collection are two Thomas Moran landscapes depicting the Grand Canyon. The more expensive of the two Moran paintings, titled The Inner Gorge, Grand Canyon, comes to auction with a $6 million high estimate. Moran’s auction record, also set in 2008, is $17.7 million.

“These paintings meant a great deal to our dad, not only because of their beauty, but because they reflected so much of what he loved about nature and the outdoors,” the Turner family said in a statement. “While it’s difficult to part with pieces that were so dear to him, our family takes comfort in knowing they will be appreciated and cherished by others.”

The proceeds from the Christie’s sale will go to the Turner Foundation, whose stated mission is to “protect and restore the natural systems—air, land, and water—on which all life depends.”

“It’s an honor to share this amazing collection with the world,” Tylee Abbott, Christie’s head of American art, said in a statement. “The quality and depth is remarkable, with exceptional paintings by Bierstadt and Moran representing the country’s lasting love of the American landscape. In the context of Mr. Turner’s collection, with the proceeds benefiting his foundation, this takes on even further meaning and will surely resonate with to day’s great interest in the American West.”

American Western art is often considered a fraught genre, since it tends to place settlers, cowboys, and explorers front and center, frequently in a laudatory and admiring way. The genre has looked especially fraught this year, on the 250th anniversary of the United States, as institutions across the nation revisited American history, sometimes with a critical eye.

But any scrutiny over Western art’s themes and images seems not to have impacted sales.

“There has long been a very committed group collecting Western art, many of them based in the West,” Abbott told ARTnews earlier this year. “In the last couple of decades there has been an upswell of interest in American art through a combination of bidders based in the West and coastal clients acquiring homes in the West.”

item.title: Anne Anlin Cheng and Patty Chang on Beauty and Violence - Hyperallergic
item.description:
When I first saw Patty Chang’s short film “Melons (At a Loss)” (1988), I was stunned by its cheeky and chilling meditation on the female Asian-American body and how it carries the weight of historic inheritance, both within the family and the nation.

The stationary camera shows Chang herself, waist up, dressed in nothing but a 1940s-ish cone-shaped “bullet bra.” (Already, femininity flirts with aggression.) Chang places on the top of her head a ceramic plate that she tells us she inherited from a dead aunt. As she balances the plate, she verbally narrates the history behind this commemorative (that is, unusable) porcelain plate, with its poisonous dye. With this object, Chang references not only a familial and feminized legacy, but also a much larger and longer heritage of porcelain as a historically transglobal commodity of Euro-American desire, and how that material desire has shaped Western conceptualization of Asiatic persons and things from the 18th century to this day. The weight of these multiple layers of legacy, Chang suggests, has conscripted the Asian-American female body, its physical and affective comportment. 

But Chang’s intervention gets even darker. As she talks, she raises a large paring knife with her right hand and begins to saw, with great difficulty and persistence, her bra-covered left breast. This act of self-mutilation lasts for almost a full, unbearable minute; we are only offered some relief when Change finally peels back the severed bra cup to reveal a real melon (a visual and verbal pun). Chang then proceeds to scoop out the innards of the melon flesh with a slightly too-large spoon and feed herself with it, even as she continues to try to talk. This act of self-feeding (or self-cannibalism?) turns a gesture of nourishment into one of violence; Chang’s movements gain speed and become increasingly frantic as she shoves the food down her mouth between words and garbled breaths.

item.title: Art Basel Paris to Give Galleries a 20% Discount After Early Closure - Hyperallergic
item.description:
After closing two days early last month, citing the ongoing nationwide protests in France, Art Basel Paris announced today, November 11, that all galleries would receive a 20% discount on their final invoices.

Art Basel Paris director Karim Crippa sent a letter to all participating galleries announcing the discount, describing the partial compensation plan as "a fair and considered way forward," per ArtNews. While the invoice reduction reportedly applies to booth fees, it does not apply to third-party expenses that the fair did not cover, such as lights, custom layouts, and special order services. Final invoices are typically issued within a month of a fair's end date.

Art Basel Paris has not replied to Hyperallergic's immediate request for comment.

item.title: Art Problems: Should I Get an MFA? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
I’m a 33-year-old painter living in New York City who makes a living as an art handler. I have about $30K in loans, plus credit card debt. I’m thinking about applying to Yale, Columbia, and Hunter to do my MFA. I want to have the option to teach, make better art, and expand my community. However, I could be spending more than $200K if I go to the Ivy League. Do I need an MFA? —Dazed and Degreeless

If aliens with basic math skills came down from space and were informed of this scenario, they’d say you were nuts for even considering getting an MFA. And yet, in this industry, we spend a lot of time waxing poetic about how important art is to the culture and how capitalism shouldn’t decide its value. So, of course we need art schools, whatever they cost.

But let me ask you this: Do you want to spend the rest of your life in crippling debt? If it’s a price you’re willing to pay, then sure — that MFA is a great idea. If not, maybe it’s time to let go of the hope that the education you get is going to pay off financially.

item.title: Contemporary Beadworker Ken Williams Jr Awarded Rakow Commission by Corning Museum of Glass - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The Corning Museum of Glass selected Northern Arapaho and Cattaraugus Seneca artist Ken Williams Jr as the recipient of the 2026 Rakow Commission. Williams began learning beadwork at an early age on the Cattaraugus Seneca Indian Territory and later refined his technique alongside master beadworkers from his mother’s Northern Arapaho family.

Widely celebrated for his pictorial beadwork, Williams used the Commission as an opportunity to move beyond functional and wearable forms, creating a standalone wall panel. Utilizing 68 different colors from a range of historic to contemporary made beads, the framed composition features a graphic depiction of the artist’s cat, Valentino, complete with thought bubbles depicting his favorite foods as part of his “Yum Series.” In centering imagery of his cat and favorite foods detailed in bold colors and expressive lines, Williams is actually presenting a self-portrait through the work.

“Beadwork is something I grew up with. It is both familiar and comforting, carrying generations of knowledge passed down through my heritage. To have this traditional art form recognized through the Rakow Commission is deeply meaningful. I’ve always used glass beads to tell stories, but experimenting with a new vehicle and format gave me the freedom to try something fresh and personal. Glass beads allow me to honor my ancestors while pushing my practice toward the future, and I’m thrilled to be able to bring that spirit to CMoG.”

— Ken Williams Jr

Now on view in the Museum’s Contemporary Art + Design Gallery, I Am the Hungry Cat, draws inspiration from Pop Art and a vibrant color palette and bridges ancestral artistic traditions with a playful contemporary sensibility, expanding the possibilities of glass as a medium for narrative art. 

The Rakow Commission is one of the most prestigious annual awards for artists working in glass and supports the creation of a new work by encouraging artists to venture into technical or conceptual projects that they would have been unable to explore due to financial limitations. The annual program was endowed by the late Dr. and Mrs. Leonard S. Rakow, who were Fellows, benefactors, and dear friends of the Museum.  

In its 40th year, the annual award was first presented in 1986, and recipients ranged from emerging to established artists including Te Rongo Kirkwood, Charisse Pearlina Weston, Leo Tecosky, Preston Singletary, Silvia Levenson, Klaus Moje, and Lino Tagliapietra.

Learn more at info.cmog.org/rakow-commission.

item.title: Anonymous Was A Woman 2026 Recipients Include Kay WalkingStick, Trisha Baga, and Beatriz Cortez - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The New York–based Anonymous Was A Woman has announced the 2026 recipients of its annual awards, which come with $50,000 each for this year’s 15 winners.

The 2026 cohort includes Kay WalkingStick, a painter whose work examines the American landscape from the point of view of Indigenous people, and Trisha Baga, whose video installations look at the relationship between the physical and digital worlds. Born in 1935, WalkingStick is this year’s oldest winner, while Baga, who was born in 1985, is the youngest recipient.

Other winners include Beatriz Cortez, whose sculptures engage speculative futures and multiple temporalities; Elisabeth Kley, who is known for her ceramic installations that feature geometric and plant motifs; and Candace Hill-Montgomery, whose experimental practice since the 1970s has synthesized “her experience of post-war segregation in New York and the revolutionary activism of the time,” per a release, and was recently showcased in MoMA PS1’s Greater New York quinquennial.

“At a time when artists face mounting uncertainty within a fast-changing world, the need for direct, unrestricted support is as urgent as ever,” AWAW founder Susan Unterberg said in a statement. “The artists that we recognize this year are extraordinary. The range, ambition, and originality of their work is a reminder of just how vital artists are for our world.”

In addition to the awards, the organization also announced the launch of the second edition of its Artists Speaks Survey, in partnership with SMU DataArts and journalist Charlotte Burns. The 2024 edition collected responses from some 1,200 artists, and the new edition seeks to “examine what has changed—and what has not—while addressing emerging challenges including artificial intelligence, changes in policy and funding, and the conditions artists need to sustain their practices.” The survey is open to women, trans, and nonbinary artists of any age; responses will be accepted until January 3.

Since 1996, the AWAW awards have disbursed over $10 million in funds to more than 400 artists. Last year’s winners included Candida Alvarez, Park McArthur, and Lola Flash. The awards are meant to support the careers of mid-career women, trans, and nonbinary artists “at a significant junction in their lives or careers to continue to grow and pursue their work,” according to a release.

“Receiving this award was incredible news. I was literally calculating the astronomical cost of hard drives to back up my digital archive when I received the call,” Baga told ARTnews in an email. “As you might know, hard drive prices these days are insane because of AI data centers driving up the demand, and I am a video artist with about 80 terabytes of very important, very tenuously stored video files I’ve gathered and metabolized over the past 20 years.”

Textile artist Elaine Reichek echoed Baga’s sentiment about the rising cost of making art, saying, “The amount is significant enough to make a real difference in my day-to-day practice. I’m truly grateful to be able to afford the cost of my materials, which have risen due to tariffs and supply chain difficulties. A burden has been lifted!”

Baga added that she will also use the funds to continue focusing on her “recently revived 3D video installation practice, providing an income so I can focus on the several institutional shows I have scheduled this year.”

“This award comes at the end of a long year, a year of big works with very limited resources,” choreographer nora chipaumire told ARTnews. “Receiving this individual award validates my life in the arts. It means recognition of an artist who wants to continue to shift frames and push over the edges. This award says to me: people matter. Massive joy and gratitude.”

The full list of winners follows below.

Laylah Ali (b. 1968, Buffalo, New York; based in western Massachusetts)
Trisha Baga (b. 1985, Venice, Florida; based in Queens, New York)
nora chipaumire (b. 1965, Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe; based in New York)
Beatriz Cortez (b. 1970, San Salvador, El Salvador; based in Los Angeles and Davis, California)
Ellie Ga (b. 1976, New York; based in Lisbon)
Andrea Geyer (b. 1971, Freiburg im Breisgau, Germany; based in New York)
Candace Hill-Montgomery (b. 1945, New York; based in Bridgehampton, New York)
Elisabeth Kley (b. 1956, New York; based in New York)
Laura Parnes (b. 1968, Buffalo, New York; based in New York)
Marsha Pels (b. 1950, Brooklyn; based in Brooklyn)
Elaine Reichek (b. 1943, Brooklyn; based in New York)
Katherine Sherwood (b. 1952, New Orleans, LA; based in San Francisco Bay Area)
Sara Siestreem (Hanis Coos, b. 1976, Springfield, Oregon; based in Portland, Oregon)
Rea Tajiri (b. 1958, Chicago, IL; based in Philadelphia)
Kay WalkingStick (b. 1935, Syracuse, NY; based in Pennsylvania)

item.title: RM’s SFMOMA Show Changed My Mind About Celebrity Curators - ARTnews.com
item.description:
An exhibition co-curated by a K-pop superstar isn’t the kind of show most art critics rush to review. But I couldn’t resist. Call it curiosity, or perhaps a little FOMO. Even my preparation for writing this review felt different: Instead of poring over essays by art historians and curators, I scrolled through fan-made reels, virtual walkthroughs, and videos featuring excerpts from RM’s audio guide. By the time I arrived, the show already felt strangely familiar.

The numbers alone make it a sensation. Since “RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me” opened in San Francisco last month, more than 66,000 tickets have sold, advance sales ran six times higher than for any previous San Francisco Museum of Modern Art exhibition, and merchandise vanished within hours. In Korea, the show has become a major cultural story. Yet when I pitched this review, the art press had given the exhibition surprisingly little critical attention. Everyone was counting the crowds. Who was looking at the walls?

I understand the reluctance. Celebrity sells, and famous names increasingly anchor exhibitions through their collections, their art, their merch. When fame becomes the main draw, what happens to the art?

RM, born Kim Namjoon, is harder to dismiss. After a 2018 visit to the Art Institute of Chicago exposed how little he knew about Korean artists, he began looking, learning, and collecting. His museum visits, shared through vlogs and social media, have sent fans on their own “RM Tours” around the world. Now, with SFMOMA curators América Castillo and Hyoeun Kim, he has arranged nearly 180 works from his collection and the museum’s holdings across eight rooms organized around color, home, friends, and people. Can personal taste carry a museum exhibition?

The exhibition starts strong. The first gallery, “Bluewater,” opens with Kim Whanki’s 1970 field of tiny blue dots, a painting that the artist’s widow donated to SFMOMA. Around it, blue keeps changing shape: Yves Klein’s saturated pigment, Kim Tschang-yeul’s water drops, Tony Feher’s plastic bottles, Roni Horn’s thick glass, uncannily like water or ice. Color is a loose, even obvious, curatorial thread, but it works on the eye: The same blue reads as weightless, liquid, dense, or impossibly still. In his audio guide, RM marvels that a painting by a Korean artist who died in New York could bring together him, the museum, and strangers from around the world.

“Friendscape” trades serenity for charm. Ugo Rondinone’s rough-hewn bronze fish hang overhead; below, old Korean wooden geese sit on a rippling, water-patterned floor, each bird differently carved, like an eccentric relative. Tiny objects perch on tiled pedestals resembling Korean floor cushions. In the exhibition’s audio guide, RM speaks fondly of the geese, traditionally associated with weddings, as objects that make him feel at home. Tigers and other animals populate the surrounding paintings and ceramics, while Lee Daiwon’s speckled Bugaksan Mountain (1976), RM’s first acquisition, recalls the Pointillist paintings of Seurat that had enchanted him.

In “PhotoBuddha,” visitors take selfies beside Nam June Paik’s television-watching Buddha, a cheeky mirror for our screen-obsessed lives, while a solitary Buddha by Kwon Jinkyu keeps to its corner. RM’s hand is everywhere: handwritten Korean wall texts, polite “please do not touch” signs, an audio track full of laughter and the occasional ramble. One gallery is titled, simply, “I Don’t Know But I Like It.”

That title is either the show’s weakness or its manifesto. I suspect it’s both. Critics are trained to look beyond mere liking. But fandom begins there: you fall for something first and study it later. RM’s audience will learn the story of a wooden goose the way they learned the lore behind an album, because someone they trust cared first. As a critic, I found that oddly nostalgic. It’s how most of us started.

The show is at its best when RM turns that openness on himself. “Home” resembles a living room: worn wooden furniture, shelves of ceramics, a sofa, small paintings, a suspended light by Minjae Kim. Chang Ucchin and Park Soo Keun keep domestic company with Giorgio Morandi. Then comes Son Sangki’s Artificial City–Irony (1987), a lavish living room with a painting hanging on its wall. Son, who lived with a disability and endured considerable hardship, often painted Seoul neighborhoods facing redevelopment. Now his canvas hangs in an interior much like the one it depicts. “Am I being a boring rich person?” RM asks, questioning his own privilege. “It makes me really uncomfortable, and I like it.” The display’s comfort suddenly becomes its critique.

In “Passion,” that discomfort deepens. A spare Park Rehyun abstraction, its floating form resembling a sail or moon, looks effortless. It wasn’t. Park raised four children, helped her deaf husband, the painter Kim Kichang, communicate with others, and painted after everyone slept. Rhee Seundja, who left three sons in wartime Korea to pursue painting in Paris, imagined each brushstroke as a spoonful of rice for her children. Suddenly, her repeated marks suggest separation, labor, and longing. Biography risks flattening complex practices into inspirational stories. Yet listening to RM reflect on his privilege in light of their perseverance, I understood why visitors were moved. The exhibition’s curators told me some visitors had cried, and that more than 700 post-visit comments had been submitted to the museum’s digital mural.

The exhibition begins in blue and ends in umber. In the final room, Yun Hyong-keun’s dark vertical bands bleed into the canvas beside a Rothko. Yun has long been introduced as the “Korean Rothko,” a convenient Western shorthand that RM challenges simply by hanging the two side by side: Rothko’s color hovers and dissolves at the edges, while Yun’s sinks into the cloth, dense and earthbound. The histories differ, too. Yun survived war, imprisonment, and the threat of execution, and his paintings carry that weight. RM admits he cannot fully grasp what those dark stains have swallowed. After the geese and the selfies, it’s an unexpectedly grave farewell, and proof that a fan’s taste can do critical work.

The timing is striking. The show opened days after Ha Chong-Hyun’s retrospective at the Asian Art Museum and the Samsung-backed “Korea” exhibition at the British Museum, and a week before Haegue Yang’s Dia Beacon commission. Korean art’s moment rests on decades of scholarship, institutional effort, and corporate and government backing. RM brings what none of that could guarantee: an audience ready to follow him.

Of course, BTS fans come first, and that should give us pause. A collector’s taste is no substitute for art history. Once it enters a museum, private taste gains public authority, shaping which artists get seen and, potentially, how their work is valued. Star-driven exhibitions shouldn’t become a museum habit. Yet the usual objection, that fame eclipses the art, misses what works here.

RM isn’t standing in front of the paintings. He’s pointing at them. His personal voice brings viewers close enough to form attachments of their own. We don’t always know why we like something. Sometimes that’s where looking begins.

item.title: Museum Organizations Call Bipartisan Infrastruture Bill a ‘Sweeping Assault’ on Historic and Sacred Places - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Some historic preservationists are alarmed at the potential effects of a bipartisan bill whose sponsors say it aims to cut red tape for infrastructure and energy production projects.

On Monday, the US Senate advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (S.5653), introduced by Senator Shelley Moore Capito, a West Virginia Republican, by a vote of 73–25. The bill is cosponsored by Senators Mike Lee, a Utah Republican; Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat; and Martin Heinrich, a New Mexico Democrat. (The current session of the Republican-controlled Senate runs through December 18; new senators will be sworn in on January 3.)

Crucially, the act would narrow the scope of the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), in part by limiting which types of projects trigger review.

Speaking on the Senate floor Monday, Capito said that “for far too long, critical investments in our nation’s infrastructure, energy production, and economy have been forced to sit on the sidelines due to endless red tape, duplicative reviews, and regulatory uncertainty.” Data from the National Association of Manufacturers, she said, “shows that permitting delays are costing America’s manufacturers $12.1 billion every year, including $87 million in additional costs in West Virginia alone. According to new data from McKinsey, $1.8 trillion of investments are locked up in the federal permitting system right now, including $22.3 billion of sidelined investments in my home state of West Virginia.”

According to the Art Newspaper, about 800 protesters gathered on the West Lawn of the US Capitol, among them leaders from the Association of African American Museums, the DC Preservation League, the American Institute of Architects, and the Archaeological Institute of America. Representative Melanie Stansbury, a New Mexico Democrat, called the act a “dirty deal.” Critics cited by the paper noted that the senators introduced the 500-page bill just 48 hours before the Senate vote was scheduled.

S.5653 targets Section 106 of the NHPA, which requires federal agencies to consider the impact of federally funded building projects and requires those receiving federal funds or permits to consult with tribal nations. According to the Art Newspaper, the new bill would make consultation with tribal nations optional and remove the requirement that federal agencies notify and consult with the public and tribal nations about potential harm to historic sites. It would also narrow the definition of what constitutes a historic site.

On November 6, the 106 Strong Coalition, which includes more than 1,200 organizations, tribal nations, and advocates, sent a letter to Congress calling for the defeat of S.5653. Signatories include the American Alliance of Museums, numerous state museum associations, and many individual museums. The letter calls the bill “a sweeping assault on the protections Congress enacted sixty years ago to ensure that federal agencies consider the consequences of their decisions for America’s historic and sacred places.”

item.title: Gochman Collection Builds a Home for Native Art in Westchester - Hyperallergic
item.description:
KATONAH, NY — In 1680, English colonists bought the land that would become Bedford, New York, from a Munsee Lenape sachem named Katonah, meaning “great hill.” Today, his name belongs to a Westchester village that is now home to Branchline, the Gochman Family Collection’s (GFC) new gallery and studio space, which opened to the public on November 6 with Line Break, an exhibition of works drawn primarily from its holdings of contemporary Native American art.

Since its founding in 2021, GFC has collected over 800 works with support from Native and non-Native gallerists, artists, and curators alike, including Creative Director and Curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít), curator and Hyperallergic contributor Shándíín Brown (Diné), and Director Laura Phipps, who also serves as Branchline’s director. Designed by Elizabeth Roberts Architects, the new space occupies two historic storefronts steps from Katonah’s Metro-North station, with free-admission galleries, skylit artist studios, a community ceramics studio, and apartments for invited artists.

Branchline makes a public home for what has essentially been a lending operation: According to GFC, more than 260 of its works have appeared in over 100 exhibitions at institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and The Broad, and it charges no loan fees. That model speaks to a known problem with private collecting, explained Joseph Pierce (Cherokee), professor and founding director of the Native American and Indigenous Studies Initiative at Stony Brook University. “Just because you collect something doesn’t mean you’re going to show it,” Pierce told Hyperallergic. “The risk is that it doesn’t circulate.”

item.title: Mamdani Begins Reconstruction of Historic Chinatown Building Decimated in 2020 Fire - Hyperallergic
item.description:
On Monday, November 9, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, along with the commissioners for the departments of design and construction, citywide administrative services, and cultural affairs, commenced the $184 million reconstruction project of 70 Mulberry Street, a historically significant building that sustained severe damage from a fire in 2020.

Upon the project's expected completion in 2030, 70 Mulberry Street will house or provide additional space for the five community organizations that operated there before the fire, including the Museum of Chinese in America (MOCA). The new building will include artist Jennifer Wen Ma's "Wings of Everchange 易之翼," a permanent, three-part art installation commissioned by the Department of Cultural Affairs’ (DCLA) Percent for Art program.

Working between Beijing and New York City, Ma has produced varied interdisciplinary media ranging from "cleansing walks," which appear like one-person funerary processions, to collections of plants coated in Chinese ink.

Designed by Grimshaw Architects, the new building retains architectural traces of the 1892 building, while expanding to include six community rooms, multipurpose areas, outdoor spaces, and several modern accommodations. The renovated building is expected to provide approximately 30% more public space than the original facility and will extend three floors higher.

Founded and constructed in 1892 as Public School 23, the building was repurposed into a community hub in the mid-1970s. After the fire devastated much of the building's structure in 2020, the five organizations operating there relocated to nearby venues. While MOCA had moved to its 215 Centre Street flagship in 2009, it retained the old gallery space at 70 Mulberry Street as an archival space and research library for the museum's 85,000-item collection, most of which was salvaged from the fire.

Since accepting a $35 million city capital grant tied to the construction of a Chinatown jail in 2019, MOCA has come under intense scrutiny. In July, protesters condemned museum leaders for accepting the so-called "jail money" in exchange for their complicity in the jail's construction and the possible devastation to Chinatown's communities.

Ma's public installation touches upon much of the Mulberry Street site's historical record and its role in Chinatown in three capacities.

The central sculpture in the building's atrium will be modeled after the graceful brushstrokes of Chinese calligraphy and incorporates salvaged materials from the 2020 fire. Within the sculpture, glass orbs serve as time capsules dedicated to certain individuals or groups touched by 70 Mulberry Street. Ma also plans to launch a publicly accessible website and app with oral testimonies from 70 community members about the building. The third part of the installation extends to the historic spiral stairwell, where ink paintings on glass panels snake up several floors along the inner stair tower.

The New York City Public Design Commission unanimously approved Ma's design in January 2024 as part of the Percent for Art program, which mandates that 1% of eligible funds for city-backed construction projects be spent on public artworks.

"Our community has gone through so many challenges and changes," Ma said in a statement. "I set out to make a work that would embrace these changes, honoring our history, anchoring us in the present and taking us soaring into the future.”

item.title: Mrs. Gallery Marks 10 Years of Getting Art Collectors to Queens - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Maspeth has not traditionally been thought of as an arts hub like Bushwick or the East Village, but one gallery has thrived by drawing collectors from all over the world to Western Queens.

“We’ve had people stop here on the way to the airport and end up buying something,” Mrs. Associate Director Lily Frances Pendery told Hyperallergic. “We had an advisor who recently spent an hour and a half with us. Anyone who comes in the door is serious about what their visit is for.”

From its leafy one-way street near the Long Island Expressway, Mrs. has worked with dozens of emerging artists, held 72 shows, and traveled to art fairs in Paris, South Korea, and across the country. This fall, the gallery is celebrating its anniversary with DECENNIUM: Ten Years at Mrs., a rotating exhibition of 30 works by 23 artists.

item.title: Mexican Duo RojoNegro Installs Colossal Work on UC San Diego Campus - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Sometimes, the best lessons are taught outside the classroom. Though still embedded on a college campus, a new artwork in San Diego brings a wealth of Mesoamerican history to the public commons, imparting ancient customs and knowledge that resisted colonial extinction efforts to the next generation.

A permanent outdoor artwork by RojoNegro, the duo representing Mexico at the 61st Venice Biennale, was recently unveiled on the University of California, San Diego (UCSD) campus. Comprising 260 unique, hand-painted ceramic tiles mounted on four tree-like panels, “La asamblea del barro” (2026) probes the transmission of cultural memory across generations by drawing on the relationship between Mesoamerican and Western knowledge that is inextricably connected through colonialism.

Hailing from Michoacán and based in Mexico City, RojoNegro artists and life partners María Sosa, who has Purépecha roots, and Noé Martínez, whose family origins trace back to Mexico's Huasteca region, use their multidisciplinary practice to bring Indigenous ways of being to the foreground. Together, they disrupt dominant colonial narratives and legacies by invoking the ancestral knowledge imbued in materials and practices that have endured four centuries of violent erasure.

“In 'La asamblea del barro,' we include the four cosmic trees that sustain the universe in Mesoamerican thought, an idea that lives on among our Indigenous peoples and bears witness to a cultural and ideological resistance that reveals the profound relationship between the body, its surroundings, and the forces of nature,” RojoNegro explained in a statement on the artwork.

item.title: Man Who Discovered Renaissance Church Facade Hidden in His House to Receive €1 M. Reward - ARTnews.com
item.description:
When Juan Francisco León Catena bought an old house in southern Spain, he expected that a planned renovation would incur costs. What he came to learn was that a Renaissance church facade was hidden behind the walls—and that it came with a reward worth more than €1 million ($1.2 million).

The discovery dates to November 2016, when León Catena and his father began tearing down interior walls in a property he’d purchased in Úbeda, a historic town in Andalusia that, together with neighboring Baeza, was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. Behind the plaster and partitions, they found an enormous stone facade measuring roughly 49 feet wide and 36 feet tall.

The stonework turned out to be part of the chapel of the former Hospital of San Jorge, also known as the Hospital of Pero Almindes, which was founded in 1347. The surviving facade includes Renaissance additions attributed to Andrés de Vandelvira, the 16th-century architect responsible for some of the region’s most celebrated buildings.

According to El País, heritage officials who examined the discovery praised its remarkable state of preservation and artistic value, describing it as a rare example of Renaissance funerary chapel architecture.

The discovery also brought León Catena’s renovation plans to a halt. Under Spanish heritage law, the facade is protected, meaning any alterations to the property are subject to strict restrictions. But the same legislation, passed in 1985, also provides financial rewards for people who accidentally discover historically significant objects or structures during construction or demolition work.

Getting that reward proved more complicated than finding the facade.

The regional government initially refused to pay, setting off a legal battle that dragged on for years. Spain’s Supreme Court has now settled the dispute in León Catena’s favor. Now, nearly a decade after the discovery, an Andalusian government valuation committee has determined that León is entitled to more than €1 million. He has yet to receive the money.

The monument itself, meanwhile, remains in limbo. León Catena has been negotiating with local officials over a plan to expose the facade to the street, allowing residents and tourists to see it. In exchange, he has proposed that the city cover the cost of renovating the four-story building.

But time may be running out. A conservation report commissioned by the regional government warned that leaking roofs in adjoining municipal properties have caused water damage, rotting wooden beams, and mold. The deterioration, officials said, could eventually lead to a structural collapse.

“Every month that passes without action increases the concern,” León Catena told El País, adding that the authorities have been warned about the risks but have yet to agree on a solution.

For now, the facade is cordoned off, essentially as it was when León Catena discovered it in 2016. He and his family, who had originally hoped to make the building their home, have since moved into another building on the same street.

“Too much time has passed,” León Catena said. His priority now, he added, is to make the long-hidden monument accessible to the public.

item.title: Oxford University Museum Returns 39 Sets of Ancestral Remains to Naga People of India - ARTnews.com
item.description:
At a ceremony held on November 9, the Pitt Rivers Museum at Oxford University in the UK formally returned 39 sets of ancestral remains to the Naga people of India. The remains, primarily human skulls, were taken during the British colonial rule of India and Burma (now Myanmar) and have been in the museum’s collection for more than 100 years. A delegation of almost 30 community members from Nagaland, an Indian state bordering Myanmar, traveled to Britain for the handover.

The Pitt Rivers claims to hold the largest collection of Naga artifacts in the world, most of which were acquired by John Henry Hutton, an anthropologist and colonial administrator in the Indian Civil Service, and a second administrator/anthropologist, James Philip Mills, between 1910 and 1940. Within that collection, 219 items are listed as Naga human remains, including 39 ancestral human remains and 178 objects that contain, or may contain, human hair. (The current return concerns only the 39 ancestors.)

On its website, the museum notes that colonial “collecting” was “often bound up with the structures of colonial violence; remains and objects were frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given.” Mills, who wrote three monographs on Naga culture and practice, refers to at least one armed expedition to demand “headhunting trophies” from Pangsha village, remarking that the Pitt Rivers would thus “get some fine specimens.”

While the Naga people practiced headhunting at the time, taking the severed heads of enemies as trophies, they also kept and cared for the heads of their own chiefs. According to anthropologist Dolly Kikon (a member of Nagaland’s Lotha-Naga community, now at the University of California, Santa Cruz) one of the remains being returned is a chief’s skull.

The Pitt Rivers removed all human remains, including those of Naga people, from display in 2020, publicizing the removal. Sensing an opening, Kikon contacted the museum’s director, Laura Van Broekhoven and offered to connect her with the Naga community. The return is the culmination of the museum’s six-year collaboration with Naga partners, which included the Forum for Naga Reconciliation (FNR) together with tribal Hohos, elders, churches and communities.

Naga tribal leaders plan to bury the remains together in a joint memorial park. “They’ve been here in a foreign land for more than a century,” said Dr Vihuto Asumi, President of the Sumî Hoho Naga tribe. “We believe that their spirits are still not at rest, so by doing this, we believe it will bring spiritual healing, not only to the ancestral remains here but to everyone who died during the headhunting days.”

item.title: Susan Silton's Loud and Proud Whistle - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — Susan Silton’s four-decade retrospective at the Los Angeles Municipal Art Gallery documents her multifaceted investigations into queerness, illness, the environment, and the politics that surround these topics. As a conceptual artist, she works in multiple media, including prints, photography, video, installation, and performance. Focused on inclusivity and community engagement, her projects are often collaborative and participatory.

Silton was already an established graphic designer when she produced the political print “Target” (1991), which superimposes labels denoting gender, nationality, and sexual orientation onto an image of a man with a target on his back. Critical of a culture that reduces people to identity categories rather than recognizing their shared humanity, Silton later created an innovative series of self-portraits by moving her face across an active scanner. In “Self Portrait #4” (1995), she distorted her physiognomy to resemble a malleable substance, a metaphor for her belief that queerness is only one of many aspects of a person’s identity, and that it can be fluid. In a related move, she scanned and manipulated images of early 20th-century bird illustrations to create the series Aviate (1998-2000), resulting in sublime, colorful, linear abstractions that symbolize birds flying freely, no longer defined solely by their behavior or physical characteristics.

item.title: Actor Says He Removed His Mother’s Art from Venice Biennale Installation as a Pro-Israel Protest - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Actor Eric Rasmussen revealed this week that he had removed his contribution to an installation by Denniston Hill in the main exhibition of the Venice Biennale because the residency program appeared to support the “eradication” of Israel, in Rasmussen’s view.

In an op-ed published by the Jewish Journal on Monday, Rasmussen wrote that he had combined two drawings by his mother of Adolf Hitler drawn from a notebook she kept during her childhood. The resulting work, transferred to an acetate panel, was included Denniston Hill’s installation, an exquisite corpse–style work titled Chimera (2026) that is located in the Giardini section of Koyo Kouoh’s main exhibition.

The piece features contributions by dozens of past residents at Denniston Hill, which was cofounded by artists kara lynch, Julie Mehretu, Paul Pfeiffer, and Jessica Rankin, along with art historian Lawrence Chua and curator Beth Stryker, and is located in Upstate New York. Rasmussen was a resident at Denniston Hill in 2019 through the DPAA Workshop.

Rasmussen said his submission to Chimera was a 1943 drawing by his mother that he had previously enlisted in a performance staged during his Denniston Hill residency. The piece is a drawing of a mustachioed man and some numbers, along with text reading, “Mister Hitler is invaded and his spitting.” For the Venice Biennale, he added a caption in red: “Mom’s childhood drawing 1943. The Toxicity of the Past?”

“I felt like the piece reflected the work I did at Denniston Hill while, at the same time, gesturing toward our current moment,” Rasmussen writes. “Neither the ‘toxicity’ of authoritarian leaders nor the rabid antisemitism called to mind by Hitler’s image remain in the past.”

ARTnews was able to confirm that the drawing did make it on view in time for the Biennale’s opening in May by examining installation shots of Chimera disseminated by the exhibition, which closes later this month.

It appears to have been taken away by Rasmussen at some point after mid-May, when, he wrote, Denniston Hill sent an email noting that the organization was more than 70 Biennale participants who had signed an open letter that objected to the Biennale’s claims of political neutrality. The signatories said this conflicted with the controversial decision this year to host pavilions for Israel, Russia, and the United States, all of which are “current regimes committing war crimes,” the letter said.

Moreover, according to Rasmussen, Denniston Hill wrote that it was “aligning with ANGA,” or the Art Not Genocide Alliance, a group that has repeatedly protested Israel’s presence at the Biennale while also noting that Palestine has no official pavilion in the show, and never has. (Palestine is not considered a state in Italy; only countries viewed as states by Italy’s government can have national pavilions at the Biennale, per the exhibition.)

“ANGA clearly considers all of Israel to be occupied Palestine and its goal is not to oppose policies of the government of Israel but to destroy the nation,” Rasmussen claimed in his Jewish Journal essay, which alleged that Denniston Hill has “no problem blithely aligning itself with an organization that seeks that nation’s eradication without even asking for the opinions of its artists.”

His essay also labeled anti-Zionism “an assault on not only the Jewish state and Jewish history, but also on language itself,” and claimed that linking “Zionism with racism, colonialism and apartheid” was akin to “Cold War KGB propaganda.”

Without stating a precise date for the work’s removal, Rasmussen said he “wrote a lengthy email” to Denniston Hill seeking the return of the drawing. Denniston Hill obliged the request and gave back the drawing, he said.

Representatives for Denniston Hill and the Biennale did not respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Bats, Spiders, and Slime Molds Make the Close-Up Photographer of the Year Shortlist - Colossal
item.description:
More than 15,300 submissions made their way to the judges for this year’s Close-Up Photographer of the Year, setting a record for the highest number of entries in the competition’s history. From uncanny insects to slime molds to unexpected animal interactions, photographs captured by amateur and professional photographers alike highlight the diverse and sometimes surreal flora and fauna all around us.

The contest winners will be announced in January. In the meantime, a photography challenge on the theme of “Close to Home” is open for submissions through the end of the month. Explore some of our favorites from the shortlist below, and learn more on the contest’s website.

item.title: Amy Genser’s Elaborate Mulberry Paper Assemblages Undulate Like the Sea - Colossal
item.description:
Plumbing the rhythms of the ocean and marine life, Amy Genser creates undulating abstractions that evoke swells, currents, reefs, and the sea floor. The artist composes elaborate wall works from rolled mulberry paper, acrylic, and wire in which patterns move and converge across swaths of blues and greens. The closer you look, the more colors emerge.

Although reminiscent of the sea in many ways, Genser’s works defy instant recognition. At first glance, they may appear topographical, as if a luminous, clear sea is being viewed from above. The rolling forms are redolent of waves but also perhaps the way corals cluster around rock formations. Then, details draw us nearer: bulbous forms with cavities resemble barnacles, and extended shapes could be tentacles.

The artist’s play on scale, texture, pattern, and depth draw us in and keep us guessing—not unlike the many enigmas of the ocean itself. And one recent project challenged Genser to work at a monumental scale. The Macallan, a single malt Scottish whisky company, commissioned her to create a monumental piece titled “Stars Below” for its Carta Nautica Collection.

Both the bottle release and the artwork celebrate the time-honored transatlantic journey of the wooden barrels used to age the spirit, which travel to Scotland from Spain and the U.S. “Through layered textures, flowing forms, and rich colors, I brought to life a mythical underwater world shaped by movement, discovery, and transformation,” Genser says.

See more on the artist’s Instagram.
