item.title: Andy Warhol's Habibi Phase in Kuwait - Hyperallergic
item.description:
VENICE — In January 1977, Andy Warhol skipped President Jimmy Carter’s inauguration to spend a week attending tea parties and dinners in Kuwait. He was invited by the country's national arts council and held a solo exhibition at the Salat Al Funoon gallery, featuring portraits of Mao Zedong and Marilyn Monroe and an array of flower prints. Domestically, his star was fading; with fewer patrons willing to meet his high asking prices, Warhol was under pressure to enter new markets. In Kuwait, where the recent oil boom had brought an influx of cash and a tether to the West and its cultural exports, he found more than a few interested buyers.

Nearly 50 years later, contemporary artist Raed Yassin has mounted a selection of photographic mixed-media works for the 61st Venice Biennale’s main exhibition, In Minor Keys, inventing scenes from that trip from the perspective of a fly on the wall.

“Warhol of Arabia” (all works 2016–2018) uses a real event as its anchor to paint a rich fiction using Pop aesthetics. In “The Party XII,” Warhol is depicted on the floor between a sheikh and a stylish kaftaned woman; Yassin painted only Warhol in color, making his hair pink and his glasses yellow, marking him as an outsider. “The Exhibition XIII” stamps four primary-colored headscarves onto a photo of Warhol with his Campbell’s soup can multiples, modifying the super-Western imagery the artist typically favored.

“The Gulf region in the 70s was kind of a black hole. No one knew what was going on, especially culturally,” Yassin told Hyperallergic. “You hear about oil and that kind of industry, but I was interested in what was beyond, what was happening in society. This is my imagination of it, which creates a different world entirely.”

item.title: Vietnamese-American Photographer and Oberlin Professor Pipo Nguyen-duy Found Dead at 64 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Pipo Nguyen-duy, a professor at Ohio’s Oberlin College and Conservatory and a recipient of the Guggenheim Fellowship in photography, was found dead at 64 in an off-campus home on Wednesday.

ABC News reports that Nguyen-duy’s son, Daniel Jones (formerly known as Asia Nguyen-duy), has been charged in connection with a double homicide for the murder of his father and stepmother, Tran Thi Phong. Nguyen-duy and Phong were found fatally shot by local police.

“The male victim was discovered on the first floor of the residence, and the female victim was discovered on the second floor. Both victims suffered from multiple gunshot wounds,” police said in a statement on Thursday. The victims’ bodies were discovered on Wednesday.

Jones appeared in court on Thursday afternoon in handcuffs and ankle shackles. He was ordered to be held in jail, and a bail was set at $3 million. Jones was arrested on Wednesday without incident after an Oberlin resident called police to report a “wet disheveled man” at her front door. About 90 minutes before the bodies were found, police officers were called to an Oberlin College campus parking lot to support firefighters extinguishing a fire in a vehicle that was registered to Jones.

In court, prosecutor Zachary Simonoff said that Jones asked the resident to record a video of him to post online. “He told her that he did not want the police involved. In the video, he identifies himself as Asia Nguyen-duy, says he’s escaping a cult. He also says, ‘Everything I did was on my own accord and I take full responsibility,’” said Simonoff in court. “Officers went there and found two people dead apparently from gunshot wounds with blood throughout the house.” In court, Simonoff said that Jones told officers that he “killed his family” when they first spoke to him and gave the officers his father’s address.

Simonoff added that police have contacted Jones’s mother in Oregon. She told them that her son is psychotic and needs medication. A motive for the shooting remains under investigation.

The weapon allegedly used in the shooting has not been found, according to the prosecutor.

Pipo Nguyen-duy had been a professor of studio art and photography at Oberlin College since 1998. “Tragedies such as this one intrude upon our lives in jarring ways. I am simply overwhelmed with sadness, and I am deeply concerned about the impact of the devastating loss of Pipo to our community,” said Oberlin College President Carmen Twillie Ambar in a statement on Wednesday addressed to students and colleagues. “Pipo was beloved. During his years at Oberlin, he touched all of us through his passion for photography. Our community will be hurting for a very long time, and when the shock of this news subsides, we will all need to process our grief. This process will sometimes be together and sometimes alone, but we will need to take the time to do so.”

Nguyen-duy had immigrated from Vietnam in 1975 as a political refugee and went on to become an internationally exhibited visual artist. He took up photography in his late 20s and pursued it academically, receiving his MA and MFA from the University of New Mexico at Albuquerque. “In his wide-ranging body of work, Nguyen-duy considered immigration and emigration, intimacy, abandonment and decay, cultural assimilation, and the cost of war,” said a tribute post from the Guggenheim Foundation on Instagram. “And he touched people all over the world with his probing, compassionate work.”

In 2023, Nguyen-duy participated in the 15th Sharjah Biennial, exhibiting photographs of schoolchildren playing in what looks like the Vietnam countryside, with some napping on felled trees while others have assault rifles tucked under their arms.

item.title: Louvre Signs Deal with Unions, Ending Threat of Continued Strikes - ARTnews.com
item.description:
As nationwide protests continue to loom across France, with the next action planned for Saturday, October 31, at least one social grievance has been addressed at the country’s top museum. On Thursday, the Louvre in Paris signed an agreement with unions who had threatened to strike for months, reports Le Figaro and AFP.

“The signature of the agreement amounts to a positive step for the Louvre,” a museum representative told AFP.

A few months after last year’s daytime robbery at the Louvre emptied the museum of over $100 million worth of its crown jewels, a broad coalition of French unions went on strike and, until this week’s deal, had pledged to continue protesting over poor working conditions, insufficient personnel, and the handling of museum renovations. The strikes began in December and forced the museum to close entirely for a total of four days and partially for another four days. Meanwhile, unions maintained an official “notice” to continue protests as needed, signaling they were not backing down and could block the museum at any time. All told, the dispute with unions is one of the longest face-offs of its kind for the Louvre.

As part of the new deal, the Louvre pledged to hire 50 new security personnel in 2027, or about 100 new hires in total by 2028, according to Le Quotidien de l’Art and other French reports. Additionally, the museum will improve pay for certain categories of workers, including a €50 ($56) monthly raise for security staff.

“The more of us there are carrying out our surveillance duties, the more we will deter criminals from targeting our institution,” Christian Galani, a representative of the French union CGT, told AFP.

The museum is in the throes of raising funds for an over one-billion-dollar renovation that will include security upgrades, the preservation of its aging infrastructure that has fallen into disrepair, and a separate, new entry and gallery dedicated to the Mona Lisa. However, there is disagreement about the cost and scope of the major renovation, and union representatives want a say in how it is handled. “We will quickly ask for a meeting on the management and prioritization of the construction works. We still have very little visibility on the safety and security plan announced in November 2025,” Alexis Fritche, leader of the CFDT-Culture union, told Le Quotidien de l’Art.

Following the crown jewel theft a year ago, Louvre president Laurence des Cars stepped down amid staff criticism that she used a top-down management style and ignored their concerns about the building’s disrepair and lack of personnel, while spending on projects they considered lavish. The arrival of the museum’s newly appointed president, Christophe Leribault, seems to have calmed some of those tensions.

item.title: A Retrospective Introduces Francis Picabia to a New Generation—with Funhouse Mirrors and a Peep Show - ARTnews.com
item.description:
While midday crowds throng under a brilliant sky on Milan’s Piazza del Duomo, darkness gathers behind the windows of the nearby Palazzo Reale, where the vernissage for a major Francis Picabia retrospective has just begun. “Picabia. Open the Gates of Night” is curated by the artist’s great-granddaughter Anne Berest, who explained in her opening remarks that “to know [Picabia] is… to spend the night with him.” As if in a dream, the exhibition unfurls in a dusky twilight, low-lit galleries gathering works under associative themes that simulate an evening escapade with the playboy artist, evoking everything from ecstatic dance and nocturnal trysts to narcotic delirium and crepuscular epiphany.

Picabia (1879–1953) is one of the elusive figures of modern art, a Franco-Spanish painter and poet who moved freely between Impressionism, Fauvism, Orphism, Cubism, Machinism, and Dada, counting among his friends luminaries like Marcel Duchamp, Guillaume Apollinaire, Alfred Stieglitz, Erik Satie, and Gertrude Stein. Always pursuing a visual language for the forms that blossomed within his brain, Picabia believed in perpetual artistic evolution, an idea encoded in two of his oft-quoted aphorisms: “A conviction is a disease,” and, “If you want to have clean ideas, change them as often as you change your shirts.” In the exhibition, this heterodox ethos is manifest in the sheer stylistic variety of Picabia’s work, the walls a procession of representational compositions, geometric abstractions, mechanical diagrams, and syncretic paintings full of appropriated imagery.

“Picabia. Open the Gates of Night” makes psychoanalytic forays into the artist’s subconscious and daringly diagnoses his desires and disorders. The stage is set with a boyhood fixation—a gallery dedicated to “the Spanish Night,” also the title of a 1922 painting. Though Picabia was born and raised in France, his father was a Spaniard; during childhood visits to Seville, he witnessed Holy Week processionals, the rhythmic movements of Flamenco dancers, and the vital choreographies of the toreador. Emphasizing his “Andalusian blood,” the adult Picabia sublimated this self-exoticizing nostalgia into compositions on Spanish subjects. At the Palazzo Reale, an entire wall is punctuated by Picabia’s loose pencil and watercolor studies of the severe faces of Sevillian women, dark tresses piled high under lace mantillas. Across the room, a series of works showcases the persistence of dots—a common pattern on Flamenco dresses—across Picabia’s figural and abstract works, such as an untitled 1942 illustration of ballet dancers and his late geometric canvas Symbole (1950). Elsewhere in the room, comparison is drawn between photographs from the Picabia Family Archive of Andalusian architecture, with its lattice panels and arches, and the painted superpositions in Salicis, a 1929 work from his “Transparencies” series (1927–33) in which image planes interweave and interrupt one another as if in double-exposed photographs.

A later gallery, “Love Parade” (borrowing its title from a 1917 mechanomorphic painting), pathologizes Picabia’s lifelong libertinism as a response to the tragic loss of his mother at the age of seven. In their 2017 book Gabriële, the show’s curator and her sister Claire detail his all-male adolescence—he was raised by father, grandfather, and uncle—and observe that his family’s resulting nickname “les Quatre sans femme” (“the Four without a Woman”), might also be heard as “les quatre cents femmes” (“the Four Hundred Women”),” perhaps foreshadowing the vast number of lovers he courted over his lifetime.

Regardless of its roots, Picabia’s sexual drive was a galvanizing force in his work, from the machinic sketches à la Duchamp’s bachelor machine to erotic paintings such as Woman with the Bull (1940–41), which was collaged from found images of pin-up models. Picabia’s unchecked libido offers another interpretation for his “Transparencies,” which emerged at a time when, as the exhibition didactics euphemistically state, Picabia “lived through multiple loves simultaneously.”

Repeatedly, the wall texts underscore the idea that “every portrait is a self portrait.” There is a sense that the exhibition’s most significant revelation is neither synesthetic experiment nor vanguardist provocation but, merely and monumentally, Picabia himself. “Picabia. Open the Gates of Night” attempts to “escape chronology,” as Berest writes in her curatorial statement, setting aside the artistic canon and movement-based ideology in favor of character-study and lyric intuition. Despite their intrigue, these biographical reveries lose their place in history, splitting narrative threads and origin stories for bodies of work—including the “Transparencies” series—across the galleries. Rather than suggesting an overarching vision of the artist’s corpus and context, a dissolution into timeless simultaneity prevails.

Berest frames the exhibition as one for a “new generation,” the museum reimagined as a carnival or party. Within the decadent interiors of the Palazzo Reale, the exhibition operates theatrically as its own scintillating setpiece, the installation design completed by sparkling lights, funhouse mirrors, and a peep show that reveals some of Picabia’s more lascivious drawings. It’s almost as extravagant as the galas that Picabia hosted in the 1930s on the French Riviera, for which he orchestrated outrageous mise-en-scènes—zoo animals secured for “Une nuit à Singapore,” a grove of palms potted and arranged for “Un soir au Palm-Beach.” The exhibition addresses an audience for whom history has been superseded by the experiential, the embodied, and the personal. Perhaps this is as Picabia himself would have it. Another of his aphorisms, after all, celebrates the unbridled iconoclasm of an eternal present-tense: “Everything for today, nothing for yesterday, nothing for tomorrow.”

item.title: In Postwar Rural France, Alexander Calder Found Respite from Pressures of Fame and a Chance to Dream Big - ARTnews.com
item.description:
If you’ve ever looked long and slow enough at Alexander Calder’s mobiles made of wire-suspended, leaf-like metal shapes painted solid colors, you likely know that they are as much about their sculptural form and silhouette as they are about the breathing air, light, shadow, and nature all around them. They shiver, drift, and play with the unpredictable whims of the surrounding atmosphere, making the invisible ether newly visible. Calder’s alternately delicate and massive sculptures are in communion with much larger forces around us.

At Hauser & Wirth in Paris, several of these sculptures are now on view (until December 19) in the exhibition titled “Calder: François Premier.” The show focuses on the late artist’s return to France from the US from 1953 to 1954 and includes a few mobiles that haven’t been seen in over 70 years: Les Granettes (1953) and The Putney Mobile (1954).

They are joined by an upstairs gallery full of bold, abstract, and figurative gouaches made between a small hamlet near Aix-en-Provence, called Les Granettes (where the 1953 mobile was made and named for), and a 17th-century home in Saché, another hamlet in the Loire Valley, now an artist residency. The more figurative gouaches include mysterious imagery such as pyramids, pulsing, planet-like orbs and even some camels.

“I seemed to develop something new,” Calder said of this sojourn to France after a 20-year absence. His “main” home and studio remained anchored in Roxbury, Connecticut, but he ultimately spent time living and working in Saché until his death in 1976.

“Calder’s return to France in 1953 is essential in understanding his late period. He was really emboldened and really inspired by being back,” Alexander S. C. Rower, his grandson and president of the Calder Foundation, says in a film screened at the gallery. “In really an unprecedented way, he was drawing directly on the metal: fabricating, welding, crafting the works into existence in full-scale, and that didn’t happen before. It was an extraordinary moment, with fantastic works of tremendous vocabulary.”

But what had brought Calder to the French countryside in the first place, and how did the place change how he worked?

To find out, ARTnews spoke with Rower, who was 13 when his grandfather died. After he completed a quick, “energetic reading” on me, which first mistakenly concluded I had been a sculptor in my youth but was amended to predict I would become one later, possibly in my 60s, Rower started with recounting Calder’s postwar story.

“The backstory is that during WWII, all of Calder’s friends were trying to come to America and be refugees,” he told me. Calder wrote to the State Department and successfully urged them to let in artists from Europe, such as Fernand Léger and André Masson. He eventually housed Masson and his young family, who all slept in Calder’s Connecticut barn-studio. After the war, Masson insisted Calder come to Aix-en-Provence, but it didn’t take much convincing. With his wife, Louisa, and their two daughters, Calder packed their things and joined their friends in southern France by 1953.

Later that year, the Calders discovered Saché in central France, where another friend (and later son-in-law) was living: the French-American journalist Jean Davidson. Calder soon bought a house in Saché on Davidson’s land, in exchange for three mobiles. From that moment on, “Saché just very naturally evolves into this hub. They have grandchildren there, and it becomes their homestead,” Rower said.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for concision and clarity.

ARTnews: What was special and inspiring about the French countryside to Calder, that might have led to the works we’re seeing here in Paris?

Alexander S. C. Rower: I wouldn’t say that France, or the countryside, was inspiring to him. He wasn’t making works related to what he was experiencing in the village and region. He was using being there to quiet his nervous system. He’s already a super famous guy when he shows up in 1953, and he has lots and lots of commissions. He’s this worldly character, and he needs to have quietude. That’s what Saché really deeply represents. It wasn’t the architecture, the chateaux in the region.

In Calder’s own words, he said he was trying to return to the ‘medieval‘—he’s talking about simple things, like going to this one place with a wood oven for baking bread, and another place that has this flock of goats and they’re making cheese. He liked the people that had maybe more challenges in life, but also had more authenticity, and he felt he was that way. He grew up with absolutely no money. His mom was a painter. His dad was a sculptor. He had to fend for himself. So the countryside in France, it’s still quite like that.

Did that simpler life away from it all change his work?

It definitely changed his work, but didn’t inspire his work. I’d say that he then had the chance with the big open skies to dream about bigger sculpture. He also was achieving success. By 1962, he found a big industrial iron works to execute his major works. He already had a smaller one in Connecticut that was making all the big works, and now he needed one in France, and the very biggest works were executed here in France. For that first group of works completed in 1963, they were all made for his own account. He commissioned seven outdoor sculptures, because he had enough money to make what he wanted to make.

What was his studio in France like?

The wagon shed, or remise, he converted to his studio was a very small space. A highly productive space. He made so many works there of the late period. Some of the 1950s, but mostly ’60s. Most of the sculpture made in the 1960s was made in that studio. Everything else before that was made in Connecticut, which was his number one studio.

When he arrived in France in 1953, he made four outdoor sculptures, standing mobiles that you put in your garden, one of which was Les Granettes (1953). He made lots of smaller works, but he didn’t make any big sculptures [in France that year].

And yet he started to think more about making large-scale works in Saché?

Saché is this little town where Henri de Balzac used to go and write, and it’s very flat. There’s nothing mountainous in the region, and the idea of monumental sculptures coming up out of the landscape is pretty obvious. It’s big sky country. Maybe the sky, you could say, was inspiring, because a big dynamic black form against the sky is terrific.

Why did you love about this place as a child?

Seeing Calder hard at work in France was a great pleasure. To go to the foundry, and see how he talked to the guys. He loved the guys that helped him execute his works. He wasn’t dismissive. He wasn’t offhand. He wasn’t at a distance. He was really connected with them. He gave them all gouaches and stuff. The welder was the guy he really liked. He’d come bring him a bottle of wine and talk about welding.

I wonder whether they kept any of those artworks he gave them.

They’ve all sold them. They’ve all come to market, and the grandchildren have sold them for education or whatever. Calder would have loved that. It’s just as it should be.

item.title: MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Will Treat Their Holdings as One Collection in Unprecedented Alliance - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Six years ago, the director of Hong Kong’s M+ museum, Suhanya Raffel, told cultural strategist András Szántó, in an interview for the book The Future of the Museum, that in the years to come museums will need to “stand together and work to help one another to deliver a more sustainable baseline.” Collaboration, she went on, “will be a key aspect of the next chapter of museum work.” Her words seem to have been prophetic: on Friday morning in Hong Kong, M+, the Museum of Modern Art in New York, and the Centre Pompidou in Paris announced a wide-ranging cultural alliance unprecedented in its scale. At the heart of the alliance is an agreement that the three institutions will treat their respective holdings as a shared collection, curated by staff spread across three continents.

“If we succeed,” Laurent Le Bon, the Pompidou’s president, told ARTnews in Paris, during a joint interview that also included Raffel and MoMA director Christophe Cherix, “we will be more than the sum of our parts, and I think that is something quite new.”

The combined holdings of MoMA and the Pompidou mean the total shared collection will number in the hundreds of thousands of objects, and the three institutions are also stewards of voluminous archives. The collection at M+, founded six years ago, numbers around 8,000 objects, but the museum has a definitive collection of contemporary Chinese art, much of it donated by Swiss businessman and former diplomat Uli Sigg. The Pompidou houses the largest modern art museum in Europe (its holdings are a national collection owned by the French state). The potential audience will be enormous: based on current figures, the museums will have a combined 10 million annual in-person visitors and 125 million online visitors.

The collection sharing will kick off with several initiatives. Beginning in late 2027, a selection of major works from M+’s collection will be installed on long-term loan in MoMA’s collection galleries, and in 2028, a long-term Centre Pompidou gallery will also open at MoMA, with similar, parallel plans in development at the other museums. (The Pompidou is currently closed for a five-year restoration of its building and is scheduled to reopen in 2030.)

As part of the alliance, the partner institutions will, over the next five years, co-organize an exhibition exploring the complex concept of “the contemporary,” which will include works from all three collections and be presented at all three institutions; curators at the Centre Pompidou and M+ will join MoMA’s C-MAP (Contemporary and Modern Art Perspectives), a cross-departmental research program founded in 2009 with the aim of exploring art histories outside North America and Western Europe.

Additionally, a joint steering committee, made up of the three museum directors along with department heads and curators from the three museums, will begin to work on such priorities as exhibitions and collection sharing, research, conservation, and professional development. The committee will meet monthly, and there will be one major in-person meeting a year, the first of which will take place next month at MoMA. (Subsequent annual meetings will rotate among the museums.)

To a certain extent, the alliance comes out of previous partnerships between M+ and the other two institutions. In February 2025, M+ and MoMA signed a memorandum of understanding that encompassed collection sharing, joint research, and curatorial exchanges. Earlier this year, M+ and the Centre Pompidou announced their own multiyear strategic partnership, which included plans for the Pompidou to inaugurate its renovated space with an exhibition of works from both museums’ collections, followed by a presentation of that show at M+.

In the interview with ARTnews in Paris, the three directors acknowledged that the new cultural alliance grew out of the previous bilateral partnerships. They stressed, however, that it also grew out of the three institutions’ commonalities, such as cross-disciplinary collecting and a focus on the art of the present, as well as the lineage the museums form: nearly a century of collecting contemporary art, starting with MoMA’s founding in 1929 and continuing through the Pompidou’s opening in 1977 and M+’s in 2021. Raffel has acknowledged that Centre Pompidou was “one of the key institutions” that M+ “looked to that helped us guide the principles around building an institution like this for Asia.”

“We each have things that are absolutely unique in the world,” said Cherix. “Our first role is of course preservation. But how can we make those collections work harder for us and touch people well beyond the walls of our institutions?”

This alliance differs from past models such as traveling exhibitions, co-organized shows, and collaborations on specific projects, Cherix explained, in that it is a long-term commitment to building programs together from the ground up, one that will involve “bringing our teams much closer together.”

The new arrangement also aims to take advantage of economies of scale and to make things like shipping more sustainable. Raffel and Cherix pointed out that, for instance, sending parts of M+’s collection of contemporary Chinese art to MoMA for extended periods would not only allow those works to rotate through the MoMA galleries but also make them more easily available to other museums in the United States.

In a world in which museums want their collections to reflect global perspectives, sharing makes more sense than continuing to accumulate separately. “We can’t just keep collecting, so we are sharing instead,” said Raffel. This raises the bar for acquisitions: to be added to the shared collection, a work will, as Cherix put it, “need to have no equal” in any of the three collections.

“Even if we want to be devoted to the art of our time, we become a historical collection,” Cherix continued. “How can we reset that? I think this alliance gives us exactly the capacity to have a different scope, and a forward-looking vision.”

More museums have partnered in recent years to share collections, pool resources, and expand their audiences. The strategy has evolved from standard short-term exhibition loans to deeply integrated models that include joint acquisitions, shared private donations, regional networks, and long-term international exchanges. Joint acquisitions have become increasingly common since 2003, when the Whitney Museum, Tate, and the Centre Pompidou teamed up to purchase Bill Viola’s video installation Five Angels for the Millennium.

An arrangement somewhat similar to the MoMA–Pompidou–M+ model came in 2018, when Chinese Indonesian collector Budi Tek partnered with the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA) in a collection-sharing arrangement with Shanghai’s Yuz Museum, which Tek had founded. (China rejected attempts to make the Yuz Museum a public institution; Tek died in 2022.) In that case, a new foundation was formed to oversee the collection, which would live in China but otherwise travel between Los Angeles and Shanghai for temporary exhibitions. Works from LACMA’s collection, for example, traveled to the Yuz Museum in 2009 for the exhibition “In Production: Art and the Studio System,” while in 2021, 20 pieces from Tek’s collection went on display at LACMA for the exhibition “Legacies of Exchange.”

More recently, museums have agreed to be the joint stewards of certain collectors’ holdings. In 2022, around 100 works from the collection of Greek industrialist Dimitri Daskalopoulos became a shared gift to the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum and the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. In 2024, three Los Angeles museums—the Hammer, LACMA, and the Museum of Contemporary Art—jointly received some 350 works owned by Jarl and Pamela Mohn. Those three institutions continue to add to that collection, called the Mohn Art Collective (MAC3).

item.title: U.S. Pavilion at Venice Biennale Is $1 M. Short, and Its Sculptures May Be Stuck in Italy - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Despite months of controversy, the United States managed to get Alma Allen’s enormous sculptures to Venice for this year’s Biennale. Getting them home, however, is proving more difficult.

The American Arts Conservancy, the nonprofit behind the US Pavilion, is roughly $1 million short of the funds needed to cover the exhibition’s costs, including dismantling the show and shipping the artworks back to the US, according to a report in The New York Times.

Jenni Parido, the pavilion’s commissioner, has been appealing to potential donors for help. In a letter obtained by the Times, she acknowledged that the final stages of the project had become difficult.

“While we have accomplished a tremendous amount in a relatively short period,” Parido wrote, “the final phase of this undertaking has presented financial challenges that I am working tirelessly to resolve.”

The American Arts Conservancy, which Parido runs, has brought in $1.4 million against a projected budget of just under $2.5 million. That shortfall has left it without the funds to store the massive stone and metal sculptures or ship them back to the US. The problem is growing more urgent, as the Biennale is due to close next month. There’s no obvious place nearby to put them, either: the US Pavilion has no storage facilities, and the Guggenheim Foundation, which owns the building, doesn’t have room for them.

The funding troubles add another chapter to what has already been an unusually messy American outing at the Biennale.

Parido, whose previous business experience included running an upscale pet boutique in Florida, was a surprise choice to oversee the US Pavilion. The Trump administration had scrapped the traditional selection process, which relied on proposals from established arts institutions and an independent review panel. Parido got the job after being recommended by her friend Erin Scavino, who heads the State Department’s Art in Embassies program.

The organizers eventually landed on Allen, an American sculptor based in Mexico, after several artists reportedly turned down the opportunity. Things didn’t go smoothly from there.

Allen told the Times that neither Parido nor the exhibition’s curator, Jeffrey Uslip, visited his studio to see the sculptures before the show. By the time the Biennale’s preview days were over, Allen and Uslip were no longer speaking.

As for the financial predicament, Allen said he knew nothing about the nonprofit’s fundraising. His own expenses, he said, amounted to travel and a cheap Airbnb, for which he was reimbursed.

The organizers had initially pitched the exhibition’s modest price tag as a selling point, calling it one of the cheapest US pavilions ever mounted. For comparison, the 2024 American presentation cost about $5 million, while the 2022 edition came in at nearly $7 million.

The State Department provided a $375,000 grant toward the pavilion, with private donors expected to cover the rest. Parido’s fundraising efforts included a party during Art Basel Miami Beach and a dinner at Mar-a-Lago. The department told the Times it wasn’t involved in raising the money.

For now, it’s unclear what happens if Parido can’t close the million dollar gap. The American Arts Conservancy didn’t answer the Times‘ questions about what it would do if it couldn’t afford to bring the sculptures home.

Katy Siegel, who helped organize the 2017 American pavilion, had a rather pithy assessment of the situation.

“This is crazy,” she told the Times.

item.title: How Édouard Manet's Black Cat Became a Symbol of Modernity - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Every Halloween, black cats return as emblems of witchcraft, bad luck, and the supernatural. Their sinister reputations stretch back centuries: starting in the Middle Ages, people associated cats with heresy and sexual transgression, and their perceived affinity with witches intensified during the trials of Elizabeth Francis and Agnes Waterhouse and their cat Sathan between 1565-1579. 

But after the Enlightenment, 19th-century French artists and writers began to reclaim the mysterious and devilish qualities foisted onto felines as desirable. Alongside a new bourgeois pet-keeping culture, where caring for animals became associated with progress and enlightenment, bohemian artists and intellectuals began incorporating black cats into their work. The black cat became a symbol of independence and nonconformity, reflecting changing attitudes toward individualism and self-expression amid industrialization and urbanization. French writer and diplomat François-René de Chateaubriand described the cat’s modern independence favorably, stating, “What I like about the cat is his character, independent and almost heartlessness […] The cat lives alone, he has no need of society.” These inherited qualities of eroticism and defiance also became synonymous with the emerging language of modern art.

No painting or artist makes this transformation more apparent than Édouard Manet’s “Olympia” (1863). Historians like T.J. Clark have long hailed it as a “founding monument of modern art,” updating Titian’s “Venus of Urbino” (1534) with a stark depiction of a contemporary prostitute, her Black maid, and a black cat. The work provoked outrage at the Paris Salon in 1865: its subject matter, combined with flattened forms, bold color contrasts, and use of black, clearly rejected academic conventions. Critics latched onto the wiry black cat, whose arched back and luminous eyes seemed to embody the painting’s perceived vulgarity by showing what Olympia’s hand covered.

item.title: After a Museum Explores Homes Destroyed by US-Made Munitions, House Republicans Demand Information on Smithsonian’s Curatorial Process - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Two Republican members of the House of Representatives want to know more about how the Smithsonian Institution evaluates proposed exhibits after a museum display tied US-made munitions to the destruction of civilian’s homes in conflict zones.

“The Subcommittee on Delivering on Government Efficiency is concerned that the Smithsonian Institution (Smithsonian) does not properly review proposed exhibits in its museums,” says a letter to outgoing Smithsonian secretary Lonnie Bunch III, penned by subcommittee chairman Tim Burchett of Tennessee along with Georgia’s Brian Jack.

The move comes in the wake of a July hearing at which Anthea Hartig, director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History (NMAH) was grilled by lawmakers, including Burchett, who demanded to know, “Dr. Hartig, are you America first? Do you love America?” Burchett and Jack say that at that hearing, members requested information on the Smithsonian’s content review process but say the institution has failed to provide it.

The Smithsonian has been a target of Republicans since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, when he wrote an executive order taking aim at the institution. The national network of museums and research institutions receives the majority of its funding through Congress. As recently as September, the White House accused the institution of discrimation and threatened to cut federal grants.

In the letter, the congressmen direct their ire at one display in particular, which appeared in “Making Home—Smithsonian Design Triennial” (2024–25) at New York’s Cooper Hewitt. “Patterns of Life” was a commission by London-born data journalist Mona Chalabi, now living in New York, and visual investigation practice SITU Research, established in Brooklyn in 2005. Their project, as described on the museum’s website, “reflects on the experiences of three individuals whose homes were destroyed by domicide—the widespread and systematic destruction of housing due to military conflict, urban development, or social upheaval.” The United Nations, the creators point out, is reviewing domicide for potential recognition as a crime under international law.

Chalabi and SITU’s display investigated and documented homes destroyed by US-manufactured weapons during airstrikes in Iraq in 2015, Syria in 2016, and Gaza in 2023. Architectural models showed people’s homes in those three places, representing heirlooms, books, toys and other household objects to “celebrate the intimate lives within those homes.”

Chalabi and SITU’s presentation was just one of 25 projects commissioned for the exhibition, some by visual artists including La Vaughn Belle, Hugh Hayden, Joiri Minaya, Robert Earl Paige, William Scott, Amie Siegel, and Renée Stout; also on the roster were photographers, designers, interdisciplinary collectives, and others. Overall, the show aimed to “explore design’s role in shaping the physical and emotional realities of home across the United States, US Territories, and Tribal Nations.”

“The Smithsonian Institution was founded for the increase and diffusion of knowledge,” say the lawmakers in their letter. “Its content review procedures need to be sufficiently robust to prevent blatantly partisan and inaccurate exhibitions.”

In at least one way, the display doesn’t seem entirely to fit the lawmakers’ characterization as one-sided. Says the museum, “‘Patterns of Life’ illuminates the complex role of the US in this issue, as it stands as the leading financial contributor to United Nations peacekeeping initiatives, but also the world’s largest producer of arms.”

Burchett and Jack say in their letter that the installation was “originally proposed to showcase 10 New York City buildings compressed into a single room,” but that “this originally uncontroversial proposal was turned into a display of homes destroyed by American made munitions in various military engagements against ISIS and other terrorist organizations.” They object to the organizers’ wish, as they say the Smithsonian described it, “to portray American military doctrine and even America’s founding as being intertwined with ‘domicide,’ defined as ‘the massive and deliberate destruction of homes in order to cause human suffering.’”

Neither the Cooper Hewitt nor the Smithsonian Institution immediately responded to a request for comment.

item.title: Why Do Horror Films Have Such a Hold on Our Imaginations? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — Horror films may have historically been relegated to second-class status in the cinematic canon, viewed by some critics as vulgar fright fests that lack the gravitas of “serious” filmmaking. But there is no denying the captivating power they have exerted over audiences, channeling our deepest fears about life, death, the world around us, and the unknown onto the silver screen. Now on view through July at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures in Los Angeles, The Horror Show takes a broad look at the history of the genre, exploring why scary movies have had such a hold on our imaginations — and prompting a reconsideration of their place in the filmic pantheon.

It all began with a single object: Dracula’s cape. That is, the original iconic cape worn by Bela Lugosi in Todd Browning’s Dracula (1931), which the Academy acquired from the Lugosi family in 2019. “It’s been a family heirloom for several generations,” Jessica Niebel, senior curator at the museum, told Hyperallergic. “We knew we wanted to highlight it in a special way.”

Once they had this cornerstone of the exhibition, curators began to assemble a wide range of material, including costumes, props, concept art, film posters, and scripts, from horror classics (The Shining, Psycho), contemporary masterpieces (Midsommar, Get Out) and underrated gems (Tales From the Hood, The Stuff). Centering both visual and narrative artistry, the curators drew heavily on the Academy Museum’s own robust collection, as well as objects and archival materials borrowed from dozens of lenders.

item.title: Escape into Gretchen Scherer’s Maximalist Paintings of Palatial, Art-Filled Spaces - Colossal
item.description:
Gretchen Scherer’s paintings of affluent homes, studios, and libraries appear to expand before our eyes. Brimming with ornately framed paintings installed salon-style on richly papered walls, her half-imagined spaces are inspired by real places, which she infuses with a playful brightness and whimsy.

When we home in on one particular floral arrangement, framed artwork, or piece of furniture, it seems that there’s a sudden increase in how much more there is to explore. Scherer’s new solo exhibition, In Time at Monya Rowe Gallery, continues the artist’s fascination with historical interiors, from art museums and drawing rooms to palatial halls and ecclesiastical spaces.

Each canvas is devoid of figures other than those depicted in portraits, but there is always the sense that someone has been very busy. The artist leans into a kind of escapism or longing for not only elegant, luminous surroundings but a desire to immerse oneself, quite literally, in the world of art. In our era of steel, glass, concrete, and contractor gray interiors, Scherer celebrates craftsmanship and beauty.

Fantastical convergences of art history and architecture occur in pieces like “A French Cafe with Paintings,” where a Beaux Arts interior transforms into an ad hoc gallery with myriad famous works casually strewn about. Gustav Klimt’s “The Kiss” (1908-09) leans to the right, while Henri Toulouse-Lautrec’s “At the Moulin Rouge” (1892-95) sits nearby.

Working in oil, Scherer’s choice of media nods to the same used to create many of the historical examples she includes. And as we increasingly contend with barrages of digital information and generative AI, the artist inundates us instead with the purely analog and handmade. It begs the question: in another 100 years, what will humans have been producing in our time that merits the same kind of awe and respect we have for these earlier creations?

In Time opens today and continues through January 9 in New York. See more on Scherer’s Instagram.

item.title: Hell Takes the Form of State Repression in 1971’s “The Devils” - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Before Derek Jarman became known for his anachronistic, queer film adaptations of the lives of Saint Sebastian, Caravaggio, Edward II, and even the Passion of Jesus, the English artist and activist worked as a set designer. This facet of Jarman, who died from AIDS-related illnesses in 1994, has recently come to the fore with the hyped release of the 4K restoration of Ken Russell's scandalous 1971 horror film The Devils, screening at the IFC Center, Brooklyn Academy of Music, and Nitehawk cinemas in New York in the coming weeks.

Adapted from Aldous Huxley's 1952 book The Devils of Loudun and John Whiting's 1961 play The Devils, the film is set in the castled town of Loudun, France, in 1634, in the aftermath of the Huguenot Rebellions against the French state's attempts to consolidate the power of the Crown and the Catholic Church. It opens with an image of a near-naked, genderqueer King Louis XIII performing on a half-shell on a theater stage à la Botticelli's “Venus” before shifting to Loudun, the site of a famous scandal wherein Ursuline nuns reportedly experienced bouts of demonic possession. The blame for this hysteria is strategically placed on a secular priest by the name of Urbain Grandier (played by a mustached Oliver Reed), who was subsequently tried and executed for his alleged crimes.

Grandier's entrapment by his enemies comes to comment on a larger evil that comes not from one poorly behaved individual but from the totalitarian powers that knock down the town's walls immediately following his burning at the stake.

"At the time that I made The Devils, I was a devout Catholic, and secure in my faith," Russell recalled in an interview in Sight and Sound in 1995, addressing the controversies surrounding the film's highly sexual depictions of nuns, priests, and even a fallen crucifix that becomes a sex object in a frenzied exorcism-cum-orgy.

“For myself, although I am not a political creature, I always viewed The Devils as my one political film. To me, it was about brainwashing, about the state taking over,” he added.

item.title: Before AI There Was the Octopus - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Helsinki-based artist Tuomas Laitinen's exhibition, Siphon, begins with copper. A decade ago, the artist set out to trace the material’s mythologies and geopolitics, and the trail led, improbably, to the octopus, whose copper-based blood carries oxygen through the deep. That conductive thread runs through the installation at Pioneer Works, where in the cavernous Main Hall, wall-scale projections of abstracted octopus skin flood the room in thermal magentas and molten ambers.

The imagery combines Laitinen's own footage with recordings of sleeping octopuses from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology. Bodies merge into a single churning terrain. An enormous pupil blinks back at the viewer from the screen. On a stepped plinth, water-filled tanks hold Laitinen's blown-glass forms, tubular and knotted, offered as shelters for octopuses. The 86-year-old ikebana (traditional Japanese art of flower arrangement) master, Kosen Ohtsubo, threads them with bare branches, pine, yard-long beans, and peanuts strung along wire, counterbalancing the heavy projections. Overhead, “8Eternal” (2026) sends Kenyan composer Nyokabi Kariuki's voice through eight ultrasonic speakers, narrow beams of sound that surface and vanish as you move throughout the space.

item.title: Found Object Masks by Romuald Hazoumè Counter Sorrow with Sympathy - Colossal
item.description:
Tethered to the spiritual realm, blue connotes a sense of serenity and healing in Yoruba culture. It’s also the color of peace, and for Romuald Hazoumè, it’s an apt metaphor for considering the legacy of colonial violence, climate catastrophe, and the global crises transforming life today.

In My Blue Period at October Gallery, the artist meditates on the contemporary geo-political landscape through a series of masks made from plastic jugs and found objects, like feathers, netting, and hardened paintbrushes. The expressive sculptures are part of Hazoumé’s series titled masques bidons, or fake masks, which utilizes the functional structures of the vessels—circular openings for mouths, handles for noses—to form abstracted figures.

The title of the exhibition references Pablo Picasso’s blue period, which emerged from his depression following the death of a friend, and preceded the Spanish artist’s African period in which he appropriated masking traditions from across the continent. Like Picasso, Hazoumé assembles found objects into minimal forms. “My intention is always to create works where no single element is ever overtaken by another,” he says. “For me, it’s crucial that you never lose sight of the container (bidon) yet still believe in the illusion. The bidon’s presence taunts you, making you conscious that it’s you projecting that ‘face’ you ‘see’ onto those plastic materials.”

Unlike the Spanish artist, though, Hazoumé isn’t concerned with his personal experience but rather ecological destruction, genocide, and armed conflicts threatening life on Earth. While earlier works in the series depicted men and large-scale issues of migration and collapse, the newer additions center on women and particular tragedies. From “the mother in Gaza killed by a sniper while seeking bread for her children” to “the grief-stricken Russian widow, who poisoned herself after both her sons died,” the stories referenced in sculpture are a way to bear witness. Hazoumé writes:

This work I do affects me deeply. I’m not making masks for other people, I’m making them for myself, trying to translate what I feel into something concrete, which stands apart from me, but reflects my innermost feelings. While making them, I gathered ordinary names from tragic tales reported in the news coming from all corners of the globe. The story is on an endless loop; women as ‘second rate beings’, continually abused and ground down by the cruelty of men.

While evoking the Hazoumé considers blue to be a counter to the “red lines” continually invoked in war and the crimson color of blood. “I imagined a balancing ‘blue line’ to stress the need to reduce global suffering and restore some hope of positive progress,” the artist says. “We need this blue middle ground to regain sympathy for each other, to help make life worth living again.”

My Blue Period runs through November 21 in London.

item.title: Vatican Exhibition Series Centers "Fundamentally Human" Art Over AI - Hyperallergic
item.description:
An exhibition series organized by the Vatican brings together more than 100 artists — including Arthur Jafa, Jeremy Frey, and Mona Hatoum — to celebrate “fundamentally human” creativity in the face of AI's rapid rise.

Across seven coinciding international exhibitions, the Catholic Universities Art Triennale (ArtCut) centers empathy and self-reflection as the primary drivers of humanity's progress, rather than technological advancement. ArtCut's inaugural edition is assembled under the umbrella of Exercises in Empathy, expanding on Pope Leo XIV's earlier encyclical on safeguarding the human condition from AI's capacities for manipulation and delusional omnipotence.

Cardinal Tolentino de Mendonça, prefect of the Dicastery for Culture and Education of the Holy See, commissioned ArtCut's contemporary art exhibitions at seven Catholic universities across Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Italy, Portugal, Angola, and the United States.

The Triennale responds directly to the Pope's assertion that AI systems “do not understand what they produce, for they lack the affective, relational and spiritual perspective through which human beings grow in wisdom.” Within this framework, each exhibition focuses on defining facets of humanity, both physical and intellectual.

item.title: Beverly Buchanan at the Raw Edge of Art - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Beverly Buchanan was mentored by Norman Lewis and Romare Bearden, a contemporary of Ana Mendieta and Eva Hesse, and most recently featured in the 61st Venice Biennale in Koyo Kouoh’s In Minor Keys. Yet, the late artist and her oeuvre have long been understudied and underexplored.

With contributors ranging from friends, dealers, historians, curators, and contemporaries, Beverly Buchanan: Ruination and Regeneration (2026) seeks to amend this oversight. Above all, it is a testament to the North Carolina-born artist’s complexity, intellect, and sensitivity across sculpture, photography, land art, and video work. It’s also a reminder that the combined effects of racism and anti-Blackness, misogyny, and regional bias on an artist’s legacy must be counteracted, as modeled by the 18 contributors' voices in this book.

Edited by Aurélie Bernard Wortsman, the monograph begins with an introduction by Andrew Edlin, longtime dealer and supporter of the artist’s work. The essays, interviews, poems (including one by Alice Walker), and images within span Buchanan’s role in Abstract Expressionism and Post-minimalism; her activity in Atlanta, Macon, and Athens, Georgia; and her eventual departure to Michigan. An extensive selection of works is included: early paintings, zines, sketches, architectural and floral works on paper, environmental installations, and sculptures.

item.title: San Francisco’s Galleries Explore Alternative Routes for Survival - Hyperallergic
item.description:
SAN FRANCISCO — No one ever said the business of art would be easy. In San Francisco, the landscape has felt particularly demoralized in recent years. A cost-of-living crisis, paired with a seemingly absent collector base and the closure of local art schools, has spurred an exodus of artists and galleries alike. Those who are sticking around are turning to alternative models to survive and foster community, from nonprofit status to retail business.

Last year, Cushion Works, in the Mission District, acquired nonprofit status and launched a membership program to help keep the lights on. That wasn’t gallery founder Jordan Stein’s initial goal when he opened the space in 2018.

“I don’t think of it like a gallery, and I’ve never had a business model,” Stein told Hyperallergic. Instead, he said he’s interested in exploring “who has lived here, what has been made here, and what can we learn from that?”

His program includes a range of Bay Area artists, from local legends R. Crumb and Dewey Crumpler to outsiders like Betty Bailey and BJ Newton to Whitney-exhibiting artists like Grace Rosario Perkins and Dionne Lee.

item.title: Lisa Sanditz’s Seismic Sublime - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Place has always been central to Lisa Sanditz’s paintings and drawings. In the winter of 2006–7, she went to China specifically to paint the rapid growth of single-industry cities, which sustained themselves by producing and exporting items such as Christmas ornaments to Western consumers. A longtime resident of the Hudson Valley, she was aware that this part of New York State, once populated by single-industry cities, such as Tannersville and Gloversville, had become post-industrial outposts for those seeking to live within hailing distance of the expensive bustle of New York City’s five boroughs. The production of inexpensive consumer goods had left America for Asia, with its cheap labor and willingness to invest in new factories.

In her current exhibition, Missing Mountain, at Alexandre Gallery — her first in New York in more than a decade — Sanditz continues to pursue her understanding of the relationship between human intervention and the landscape, paying particular attention to fitting together different pictorial languages. This postmodern approach to landscape sets her apart from her modernist forebears, from Marsden Hartley to Alex Katz, as well as implicitly acknowledges the destructive effects of climate change and greedy, unthinking human intervention. And yet, despite this awareness, Sanditz never devolves into proselytizing. Despite the gravitas of her subject matter (the degraded landscape), her pursuit is inspired by her painterly desire to celebrate beauty and what acrylic paint, and its expansive range of artificial colors, can do. Observation, memory, and imagination are inseparable components of her thinking and doing.

item.title: A Macro Journey Underwater Reveals the Radiant Geometries of Coral - Colossal
item.description:
Armed with high-magnification macro lenses, filmmaker Sandro Bocci journeyed through coral reefs to document a striking array of color, texture, and pattern. A project for Bocci’s collective Julia Set Lab, the short film homes in on the intricacies of a life form we can’t see with the naked eye. Subtle shifts in gradients, bold color juxtapositions, and a seemingly endless diversity of recurring motifs explode across the frame, revealing the beauty and complexity of the extraordinary organisms growing below the water’s surface.

Set to music by Maurizio Morganti, “Iteration” is the second collaboration by the pair, who continue to harness the power of technology to create works at the intersection of art and science. Watch the film on Vimeo, along with additional films.

item.title: 2,500-Year-Old Mesoamerican Observatory Discovered in Sierra Norte Mountains of Mexico - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A team of researchers at the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) in Mexico recently announced the discovery of a 2,500-year-old structure that they believe functioned as a solar observatory.

The structure is part of the pre-Hispanic Teteles de Ávila Castillo archaeological site in Sierra Norte de Puebla and has been under excavation by INAH since 2015. Alberto Diez Barroso Repizo, Teteles’s archaeological project director, told the Art Newspaper that Teteles “flourished during the Middle Preclassic period (900BC-600BC) but declined around AD100, possibly because nearby Cantona expanded.” Diez points to the discovery of green obsidian beads as an indication that Teteles, which is along a trade route, was connected to the much larger Mesoamerican city Teotihuacan, since that city controlled a quarry where the obsidian originated.

The discovery indicates that Teteles’s architects and inhabitants had a sophisticated knowledge of astronomy: the observatory was designed to track the beginning of the Mesoamerican calendar in February and the harvest in October, according to a statement from INAH. One of the project’s researchers noted that the eastern base of the complex “constitutes a solar calendar,” based on observations of the trajectory of the sun aligning with the front of the structure during the beginning of equinoxes and solstices.

Diez told TAN that INAH plans to open the site, and eventually a museum, to the public.

Claudia Curiel de Icaza, Mexico’s Secretary of Culture, noted that the discovery expands the country’s understanding of its own history. “The architecture of Teteles de Ávila Castillo tells us about societies that developed astronomical knowledge and incorporated it into the organization of their ceremonial spaces,” she said.

item.title: A Painting Owned by Dutch Jewish Collector Once Hung in Hitler’s Home, New Research Finds - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A Nazi-looted painting that once belonged to a Dutch Jewish family, and at one point hung in Adolf Hitler’s home, has been traced in new research, the Dutch newspaper Het Parool reports.

The work in question is German painter Carl Gottlieb Peschel’s Joseph Sold by His Brothers (1831), which shows the biblical scene of Joseph being sold into slavery in Egypt.

The painting belonged to Bob Nijkerk, whose family had made its fortune in the iron and scrap-metal business in the 19th century. Nijkerk, who died in 1987, used that wealth to build a collection of bibliophile editions, modern Dutch typography, and paintings. He received the Peschel as a gift from his brother-in-law in 1941. When the Nazis occupied Amsterdam in 1940, he was a managing director of the family company, which the Nazis seized in 1941.

Starting in 1942, the Nazis deported more than 100,000 Dutch Jews to killing centers. Nijkerk, his wife, and their three children were spared at first. Willem Sandberg, a curator at Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum, where Nijkerk had loaned and donated artworks, intervened on their behalf and got them placed on an exception list of about 700 Jews. In 1940 the two men visited the museum’s art bunker together, and the collector likely stored important works there.

The family was first taken to De Schaffelaar Castle, about 45 minutes outside Amsterdam. They were later deported to the Westerbork camp in the Netherlands and then to Theresienstadt in what is now the Czech Republic. “Ultimately, all five survived the war because they were brought to Switzerland by train in 1945 along with a select group of camp prisoners from Theresienstadt,” Het Parool reports.

Nijkerk’s grandson Willem Nijkerk knew that his family had included bibliophiles but didn’t know how large his grandfather’s collection was. He learned of the family’s link to the painting from Diederik Oostdijk, a professor of English and American literature at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam.

“I mainly knew about the period during and after the war. Through Oostdijk’s research, I was given a glimpse into their prewar life. They lived in relatively grand luxury,” Willem told Het Parool.

Oostdijk tells the Nijkerk family’s story in his new book, Overlevingskunst (The Art of Survival). According to its description, the book follows “three Jewish families [who] miraculously escaped the Holocaust thanks to their art collections.”

Oostdijk’s research shows that the Peschel spent some time in Hitler’s Berlin home. It was then moved to Hitler’s storage facility in Munich, where prized works were held for a planned Führermuseum.

It is still unclear whether Bob Nijkerk sold the painting in late 1941 or early 1942, or whether it was confiscated later, when German forces or their Dutch collaborators raided Jewish homes. After the war, Nijkerk recovered many of his books but “never uttered a word about Peschel’s painting,” Willem said. “I don’t think he had much of a connection to the painting himself. The painting does not evoke much emotion in me either.”

Nijkerk’s seven descendants have not filed a formal restitution claim for the Peschel. They also have not claimed three other paintings that Oostdijk has linked to the Nijkerk collection: two 1633 portraits by Caspar Netscher and a 1673 painting by Gerbrand van den Eeckhout. Those three works are at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam. Joseph Sold by His Brothers is now in the Martin von Wagner Museum in Würzburg, Germany. Willem said that if the paintings are ever restituted, the family would likely sell them.

“It is a bizarre thought that a painting belonging to my grandparents was in Hitler’s residence, one of the most horrific human beings who ever lived, and to think that he found this work so beautiful,” Willem told Het Parool. “I don’t necessarily want Peschel’s painting on my wall at home. I also find it an unpleasant thought that it lay in Hitler’s home.”

item.title: Researchers Trace Vincent van Gogh’s ‘Starry Night’ to a Specific Dark Sky in 1889 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The storied Starry Night that has mesmerized countless eyes since Vincent van Gogh painted it may have been cribbed from an actual night sky over France in July 1889.

As reported by the Associated Press, “A South Korean team reported Thursday that after years of forensic astronomy and research into the Dutch artist, they have matched his masterpiece to a predawn sky over France’s Saint-Remy de Provence right around July 22, 1889. That’s a month later than the long-accepted time frame for the postimpressionist painting depicting a crescent moon and Venus surrounded by a sky of swirling stars with a village nestled below and cypress trees looming on one side.”

The Starry Night had long been thought to allude to a night in June, the month after Van Gogh checked himself into a psychiatric hospital in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in the wake of famously cutting off his ear in December 1888. But, per the AP, “a team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of a Seoul telescope maker, is now disputing that date in a study appearing in the journal Scientific Reports.”

“No two skies are the same,” Kim told the AP in an email. “Something always changes. I believe Vincent noticed those changes and put them into the painting. I am confident that July 22 is the better date. I will bet on this date.”

Another researcher who has studied the painting described the claim as “an intriguing hypothesis rather than a settled answer,” but Kim considers it concrete after having studied evidence including astronomical charts as well as mention of cicadas (insects most active in the depths of summer) in letters written by Van Gogh.

Kim also noted having never seen The Starry Night in its most singular form at MoMA in New York. “Now that the paper is out,” he said, “I really have to go and see The Starry Night in person, don’t I?”

item.title: Auction of Nazi-Looted Torah Fragment Canceled After Outcry and Israeli Government Intervention - ARTnews.com
item.description:
After an auction house in Norway attempted to sell a fragment of a Torah scroll looted by the Nazis, a public outcry ensued.

Israel’s Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar also intervened and, according to a ministry spokesperson, asked the Israeli embassy in Norway to prevent the sale, reports the Jewish Telegraphic Agency (JTA). “Thanks to the embassy’s efforts, the auction was canceled, and the parchment will be donated to a Holocaust remembrance organization in the United States,” a foreign ministry spokesperson told the JTA.

Previously, Israel’s foreign ministry had called the sale, which had been scheduled for October 18, “A Nazi celebration in Oslo.”

The Valkyrie Historical Auctions in Oslo listed the artifact on its “Historical 3rd Reich Items” online auction. The torah fragment lacks complete expert confirmation of its provenance. A description for the lot reads, “Very Old Piece of Jewish Torah Roll Plundered by SS German Soldiers During Soah and sent to a relative as a souvenir. This piece is handwritten in calfskin and damaged probaby [sic] by fire. It has the feldpost of the soldier unit written on it and directly written on it the address in Germany to whom it was sent.”

The house further described the item, still listed as lot 83 on the now completed sale, as a “sad and powerful symbol of the destruction of European Jews and their culture and tradition.” It was valued at between $1,500 and $2,000, and was won for $8,500 by an unknown bidder, though the auction house said the transaction had not been completed, according to Jewish News.

It is also unclear under what circumstances or to what extent the online auction house canceled the sale, or whether the Torah fragment was ultimately purchased from its owner and then donated. ARTnews’s request for comment was not immediately returned. According to its website, the Valkyrie Historical Auctions are “specialists in WWII and Holocaust-era artifacts,” led by historian Norbert Podlesny, who has written about the persecution of Jews during the Nazi era.

Though it has not been finalized, Remember Us The Holocaust (RUTH), a remembrance organization in San Diego, told JTA they had been working to obtain and preserve the Torah fragment using “appropriate treatment and respectful exhibition” methods. RUTH executive director Moisés Salinas Fleitman did say the organization received an email confirmation that the artifact would be donated to them, but was awaiting its finalization.

Some are now demanding further investigation into how the auction came about despite it being listed as looted, as well as broader efforts to stem the sale of plundered Jewish items. “This is not simply an antique or a historical curiosity. It is a sacred Jewish object that represents a community’s religious life and the devastating destruction of that life during the Holocaust,” Gideon Taylor, president of the World Jewish Restitution Organization (WJRO), told the JTA.

item.title: How Mexican Photographers Made a Nation - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — In “Tríptico de los martirios” (1950), the late photographer Lola Álvarez Bravo patiently renders her subject anonymous, capturing a tree’s shadow crawling toward her subject’s bare chest with exquisite timing. In Graciela Iturbide’s “Mujer ángel” (1979), meanwhile, a woman with a veil, long white skirt, and portable stereo traverses a field of flowers to encounter a spotty desert. Almost cinematic in their presentation, both works demonstrate a keen attention to light and form as well as an emotional sensitivity to their subjects, demonstrating the way modernist approaches to photography shifted the visual culture of Mexico in the 20th century. 

The work of both artists is prominently featured in Instante/revelación: Moments in Mexican Photography at the Getty Center in Los Angeles, which brings together the work of 13 Mexican photographers from the late 1920s to the mid-2010s to trace the arc from post-Revolution nation-building to contemporary life through photography. 

The exhibition takes its name from a book published by the late Nobel Prize-winning Mexican writer Octavio Paz entitled Instante y revelación (Instant and Revelation, 1982). In it, Paz pairs his poetry with photographs by Manuel Álvarez Bravo, whose work he encountered in the Mexican literary magazine Contemporáneos (Contemporaries). This relationship between language and visual art informs the exhibition’s framework, allowing for poetic groupings. In this way, artists and intellectuals, including Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera, and David Alfaro Siqueiros, are shown alongside landscapes, botanical species, and scenes from everyday life.

item.title: In Battle Over Auschwitz Watercolors, Roma Victims Are Getting Left Behind - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The decades-long ownership dispute between the family of late Holocaust survivor Dina Gottliebova Babbitt and the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum over seven watercolors depicting Roma prisoners is back in the news. That's because the dispute culminated in a California lawsuit initiated by her daughters 17 years after their mother's death.

Nicknamed the “Angel of Death,” Dr. Josef Mengele ordered Babbitt to portray the traits of Roma prisoners as part of his pseudo-scientific experiments to prove what he perceived as their racial inferiority. Under these extreme life-and-death circumstances, Babbitt created the watercolors to save her life as well as her mother's. All the Roma people forced to pose for these portraits were later executed. 

The news coverage and conversations around the ownership dispute have long missed an essential frame through which to view this tragedy: the rights and dignity of the Roma people who were depicted, killed, and forgotten. What decision would best honor them? How do we stop the harmful experiment's long-term impact from further stigmatizing Roma identity?

item.title: Playfully Vibrant Abstract Murals by Zebu Enliven Urban Walls - Colossal
item.description:
For more than a decade, Berlin-based artists Lynn Lehmann and Dennis Gärtner, a.k.a. Zebu, have been transforming otherwise mundane walls and surfaces into vivid, geometric paintings. Moving between patterns and representational abstraction, the duo draw on their adjacent work in illustration and graphic design to create eye-popping compositions. Indeed, much of their practice is studio-based, so murals introduce broader possibilities in a variety of settings. “There’s something special about being able to interrupt someone’s everyday routine with an unexpected visual surprise,” the pair says.

Currently, Zebu is experimenting with a more intuitive approach to murals as a complement to their method if planning extensively beforehand. “It’s been a really exciting and surprising experience that has taught us to trust the process more and brought back a lot of the fun of painting.” See more on Zebu’s Instagram.

item.title: Tom Hegen’s ‘The Mineral Age’ Documents the Indelible Effects of the Green Transition - Colossal
item.description:
In its current form, the global transition away from fossil fuels will depend on the earth’s rare minerals. According to ClimateWorks, we’ll collectively need to mine 6.5 billion tons of cobalt, copper, lithium, nickel, and other materials before 2050 in order to keep up with energy demands. Most of these resources are found in regions already facing the greatest impacts of the climate crisis, from Chile’s Atacama Desert to Indonesia’s nickel reserves to the cobalt deposits of the Democratic Republic of Congo.

For the past six years, German photographer Tom Hegen has been traveling the globe to document the communities bearing the brunt of this transition. Through his signature aerial images, Hegen captures the landscapes and communities transformed by such extractions, which he presents in his new book, The Mineral Age.

“What particularly caught my attention was that many of these resources are concentrated in just a handful of countries, creating new geopolitical dependencies and vulnerabilities,” Hegen tells Colossal. “At the same time, their extraction often comes with significant environmental and social consequences that receive relatively little public attention.”

The Mineral Age redresses that omission through 247 photographs revealing the indelible effects of mining. We bear witness to the candy-colored evaporation ponds needed to harvest lithium in the Atacama Desert, along with an ochre-tinged nickel pit jutting up against a rainforest in Sulawesi, Indonesia. “Moving away from fossil fuels is far more complex than we might initially imagine. I firmly believe that decarbonising our economies and societies is essential to addressing climate change,” he adds. “The pressing question, however, is at what cost—and who ultimately bears that cost?”

Hegen echoes the concerns of communities around the world, including those of the Salinas Grandes in the Atacama Desert. We recently wrote about the collaborative project helmed by Argentinian artist Tomás Saraceno, who’s been collaborating with Indigenous peoples in the region for decades as they protest lithium mining. Together, they’re working to preserve the ancestral homelands and the resources held underground. Revealing the impacts from the air, The Mineral Age is a converse to Saraceno’s project, which is embedded in the land itself.

“One of the most important lessons I’ve taken from this project is that no source of energy comes entirely without environmental or social consequences,” Hegen says. “Even technologies we consider clean or renewable depend on extensive industrial processes, vast amounts of raw materials, and the extraction of finite resources.”

Like Saraceno, Hegen also emphasizes that this conversation isn’t about whether we need to abandon fossil fuels—both agree we do—but rather about how we can do so without replicating the same harmful, extractive policies of our current system.

Published by Hatje Cantz, The Mineral Age is available for pre-order on Bookshop or through Kickstarter. Follow his latest projects on Instagram.
