item.title: Ursula von Rydingsvard, Who Sculpted Monuments of Cedar, Dies at 84 - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Ursula von Rydingsvard, a sculptor whose monumental objects were partly inspired by her childhood in post-World War II refugee camps, died in her Manhattan home this morning, October 27, at 84. The artist's studio manager, Courtney Childress, attributed Von Rydingsvard's death to Alzheimer's disease, according to the New York Times.

During her over five-decade career, Von Rydingsvard chipped away at enormous cedar beams to create a menagerie of massive sculptures, from an assembly of cones to a 17-foot-tall tornado-shaped behemoth made from 15,000 pounds of wood. The abstract sculptor worked with an array of other materials, including bronze, textiles, and animal intestines.

"She was like the sun. She was this force that pulled people in and kept them orbiting around her," Childress told Hyperallergic in a phone interview. "She moved through the studio like her hair was on fire, and could never slow down."

Born in 1942 in Deensen, Germany, in the midst of World War II, to a Polish mother and a Ukrainian father, Von Rydingsvard took significant inspiration from her childhood experiences. When the war ended in 1945, her family of nine navigated eight Nazi slave-labor and postwar refugee camps before taking a military ship to the United States in 1950, as she relayed in an interview with Art 21.

While she resisted autobiographical readings of her oeuvre, her observations of the wooden barracks in camps and pre-industrial wooden Polish homes informed her preferred medium of cedar, she continued in the interview. Other memories, from the feeling of a linen nightgown to the sun warming her body, created a reservoir of inspiration for her works.

She went on to obtain a Bachelor of Arts and a Master of Arts from the University of Miami in 1965, and earned a Master of Fine Arts in studio art from Columbia University in 1975.

Recipient of a spate of honors, including the Guggenheim Fellowship, the Joan Mitchell Fellowship, and grants from the National Endowment for the Arts, Von Rydingsvard gained widespread recognition for translating visual cues of human anatomy, the environment, and household vessels into large-scale pieces, departing from the aloof nature of 1970s minimalism. She was the subject of solo exhibitions at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, the National Museum in Krakow, and the Yorkshire Sculpture Park in the United Kingdom, and her work is in the permanent collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, and the Whitney Museum of American Art in Manhattan.

item.title: Layli Long Soldier’s Poetic Lifeblood - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Reading Layli Long Soldier’s newest publication, We (Graywolf Press, 2026), is a visual experience. She leads us across the page through poetry and storytelling, but her work is far more than ideas, statements, and wordplay. Even when just text on the page, it is both literature and visual art. Through this bridge, it creates deep connections to our innermost experiences — at times validating our own humanity, or providing a window into another’s. Fittingly, the title has two meanings: the English “we” and the Lakota “wé,” meaning “blood,” a shared lineage and life source.

Layli and I first met while we were both attending the Institute of American Indian Arts in Santa Fe, New Mexico. As fellow Lakota in the Southwest, art students, and mothers, we bonded quickly. Our now-grown children played together when they were toddlers. We have continued to support and cheer one another on throughout the past 20 years as friends and colleagues. I am thrilled to have been able to spend dedicated time with her new book. Readers will recognize the strength and unique literary style Layli demonstrated in her 2017 poetry collection Whereas, while experiencing the excitement and joy of new terrain offered in this moving body of exploratory and expansive work.

We (Wé) is life-affirming, motivating, a call to action, an instigator of deep critical thinking; it binds together our history and our present. It is advocacy and truth-telling, education, and inquiry, all through a lens of lived experience, compassion, and love. It is an artistic expression led by Lakota values and philosophy and, through this, connects to humanity at large. Our conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Dyani White Hawk: You utilize text placement, formatting, omission, symbols, color, rhythm, pauses, reader choices, and instructional language to paint rich visuals in each section of this book. There are essays and short stories, photographs, and visual art scattered throughout. You are a poet, and you are an artist. Can you please speak to the process of how you find form for a work? Do you see the shape in advance? The color? Do the words come first, and reveal their shape?

Layli Long Soldier: First of all, thank you so much, Dyani, for such a beautiful introduction to my work. And I, too, identify so deeply with your work. I think a lot about process. And in your work, I recognize the time, meticulous detail, the math, the planning, the patience, and likewise, the sensitivity to color, shape, and underlying meaning and philosophy that you put into your pieces.

Some of the forms for my poems are really demanding. They require tight use of space, down to the centimeter, at times, e.g., the poems in A Line Through Grief or Obligations. Even when the form requires every last bit of patience, believe it or not, my friends and relatives who do beadwork or detailed sculptural pieces inspire me. I think to myself, if they can sit and patiently pick up one bead at a time with a needle, then I can practice that kind of attention as well! So I keep going.

Sometimes the form in my poems does come first. I’ll wake up in the morning and I can see a shape. It feels almost as if a shape is waving hello, inviting me. So I go to my laptop with a general idea of what I want the poem to look like. And this, then, becomes the first constraint. I begin building the poem from there.

But sometimes, it’s the language that comes first. Perhaps I’m thinking about an experience, a memory, or a person, and this is where I begin. I enter the quiet mental excavation for words to translate a feeling or idea onto the page. Once the language feels right, I’ll begin the next stage of trial and error to find the right form. There have been some poems that take months or years to complete because of this process. Yet it’s so rewarding once I do find the right form, because suddenly the poem gets traction and starts to move. I can feel it in my body, it’s as if the poem says, “Thank you!”

DWH: I also really appreciate the kind, gentle, strong yet nurturing way you very intentionally lead readers through a work with commands, reminders, and encouragement. You work to ensure that they remember to hear, see, and feel what is being offered. Do you feel this is related to who you are as a Lakota artist? As a woman? As an Indigenous artist?

LLS: I’m not really sure why I do this in my writing, except it is my nature. In some ways, I consider the reader a guest. Isn’t it funny that “stanza” means room? So you could say that as I invite guests into a poem, I am guiding them through the rooms of a kind of home that I’ve built.

Also, over the years, I’ve developed an awareness that there are many ways — techniques or approaches — to help a reader feel comfortable enough to stay with me, even when I’m diving into difficult subject matter. Sometimes, I press hard. For example, in my essay “Through the Pupil of Instinct” [in We], I share painful first-hand accounts from survivors of the Wounded Knee Massacre. Yet, the essay moves multi-directionally, shifting from Wounded Knee to my child’s day at school to a drive through Minneapolis with my poet friend, Heid Erdrich. These shifts allow the reader time and breath to endure the moments of intensity. I want to say what I need to say, I want to “go there” when it comes to harm, violence, or injustice, but I also want readers to be able to sustain the energy it takes to go there with me.

item.title: Jogen Chowdhury, ‘Towering Pillar’ of Indian Modern Art, Has Died at 87 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Jogen Chowdhury, one India’s leading modern painters whose figurative oeuvre foregrounded humanity, died at a hospital in Kolkata on October 25. He was 87. Indian media reports that Chowdhury had been suffering from a rare blood cancer for more than a year.

Condolences have poured in on social media in the wake of his death. Writing on X, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari praised Chowdhury as a “a towering pillar of our cultural world,” whose artistic legacy would be “immortal through the ages.” Likewise Samir Aich, a prominent painter based in Kolkata, mourned his death as “personal loss” and representative of a chapter closing on the Bengal School of Art, an early 20th-century art movement that originated in Kolkatta (formerly Calcutta) and Shantiniketan during the British Raj, and then flourished across the Indian subcontinent, buoyed by the Indian Independence Movement.

Reacting in part against the dominance of Western realism in Indian art eduction at the time, the Bengal School of Art drew on Indian traditional art forms, such as Mughal miniatures, pastoral themes, and the intermingling of history and mythology. The distinctive red earth landscape of Santiniketan, where Chowdhury had a home, was a particular inspiration. Elements of Cubism and Japanese modern art sensibilities were threaded throughout the movement, owing to a thriving cultural exchange between India, Japan, and Europe.

Chowdhury was renowned for his line work, which excelled in the tactile, expressionistic quality unique to Indian art. He often used a cross-hatching technique to delicately distort the human figure, pushing them to caricature not as a mockery, but as a means of visualizing psychic interiors.

“The figures are wrought by a combination of decorative wilfulness and expressive distortion and are imbued with an effusive sensuality,” Indian art critic R. Siva Kumar once wrote. “Chowdhury’s art is rich in suggestions; it is to be apprehended without bracketing our fund of knowledge, experience or memories, but also cannot be narrativised without trivialising it, without depleting its sensory particularities.”

Jogen Chowdhury was born on February 16, 1939, in Daharpara village in Faridpur, then a region in undivided Bengal. (British occupying forces partitioned Bengal along religious lines for the second time in 1947, after a failed attempt in 1905.) He described a creative, aristocratic upbringing: His mother was renowned for her skill in Alpana drawings, and his father was a painter and sculptor.

He enrolled in to the Government College of Art & Craft, Kolkata in 1955. He also trained at the Government College of Art & Craft from 1955 to 1960 and later at the École Nationale Supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris in the 1960s, returning to India in 1968.

In 1972, Chowdhury served as a curator at the Art Gallery of Rashtrapati Bhavan, the official residence of India’s president. In April 2014, he entered politics, winning election to the Rajya Sabha, India’s upper house of Parliament, as a member of West Bengal’s Trinamool Congress. He served until April 2020.

Chowdhury’s art accolades include the Prix de la Jeune Peinture in Paris in 1966 and recognition at the Second Havana Biennial in Cuba in 1986. In 2001, he received the Kalidas Samman from the government of Madhya Pradesh in recognition of his artistic contributions. In 2012, he was awarded the Banga Bibhushan, the highest civilian honor conferred by the government of West Bengal.

item.title: At 60, a Legendary LA Print Workshop Still Urges Us to Pay Attention - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — Founded in 1966 by Sydney B. Felsen and Stanley Grinstein, Gemini G.E.L. has long been one of the crown jewels for printmaking. To celebrate its 60th anniversary, Gemini invited curators Susan Dackerman and Helen Molesworth to mine the archive for the exhibition (Almost) Every Year: Sixty Years of Printmaking at Gemini G.E.L. Although the exhibition covers almost every year, the curators were primarily interested in how, as a workshop, the venue served as a place for dialogue among visiting artists and for tinkering outside normal routines or comfort zones. 

As the chronology reveals, Gemini opened with a bang, bringing in celebrated New York artists such as Josef Albers, Man Ray, Robert Rauschenberg, Jasper Johns, Claes Oldenburg, Frank Stella, and Ellsworth Kelly. At the same time, they recognized the achievements of Los Angeles’s own growing artist community by inviting David Hockney, Ed Ruscha, Ron Davis, and Bruce Nauman. By the 1980s, women worked at Gemini, starting with Dorothea Rockburne and Vija Celmins, followed soon after by Susan Rothenberg and Elizabeth Murray. Today, as the curators noted in the gallery talk, Gemini’s artist list is distinguished by its gender equality.

Mutual interests among resident artists are nicely illustrated through juxtapositions that show Stella and Kelly exploring shape and color, Rauschenberg and Johns toying with found object imagery, Rothenberg and Richard Serra taking the color black to the extreme, and Toba Khedoori, Julie Mehretu, and Analia Saban examining linear matrices. Several works stand out because the artists cleverly defy our expectations. For example, Joel Shapiro and Richard Tuttle, both known for their unique approaches to predominantly minimal sculpture, opted for exuberant, polychromatic palettes and complex configurations in their screenprinted geometric abstractions. 

The best examples of experimentation push the boundaries of what we consider a print. In 1969, Oldenburg molded polyurethane to replicate an automobile profile in relief, perhaps influenced by the Southern California Finish Fetish art of the period, while Johns printed an image of a lightbulb on lead, turning something fragile into a durable, permanent object. Pushing conventions even further, Edward and Nancy Kienholz turned ordinary gasoline containers into sculptures resembling television se ts, and, more recently, Allen Ruppersberg created a multi-colored screenprint on a 20-foot-long perforated piano-player roll which he divided into four separate sections. Titled after a traditional Southern gospel hymn that was once recorded by Johnny Cash, “Great Speckled Bird” (2013) takes a nostalgic look at classic Americana. The imagery consists of reproductions of lyrics from age-old songs, handwritten by the artist on vintage motel stationery.

item.title: Bill Koch to Sell More Than $40 M. in Art at Christie’s, Led by Monet and Cezanne Paintings - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Billionaire collector William “Bill” Koch is ready to sell more of his art. After parting ways with $84 million worth of American art at Christie’s in January, he’s putting another group of paintings up for sale this November, including works by Claude Monet and Paul Cézanne that could fetch as much as $18 million apiece.

Christie’s said the collection, which also includes works by Edgar Degas, Henri Matisse, Joan Miró, and Diego Rivera, is expected to bring more than $40 million during its marquee sales in New York next month.

The announcement marks the latest chapter in what has become a very lucrative relationship between Koch and the auction house. In June 2025, Christie’s sold $28.8 million worth of wine from his cellar, followed by his Western American art auction seven months later. Both sales exceeded expectations, according to Christie’s.

And it isn’t just art and wine that Koch has been selling. He’s also been trying to find a buyer for Elk Mountain Lodge, his sprawling 52-acre estate in Aspen, Colorado. The property went on the market in January 2025 for $125 million, but after failing to attract a buyer, Koch slashed the asking price to $99 million and put it up for auction in July. The estate, which he bought for $26.5 million in 2007, includes a 16,631-square-foot main house, seven guest cabins, and enough amenities to make leaving the property seem almost unnecessary.

It’s unclear what’s behind Koch’s motivation to sell. In under two years, the 85-year-old has parted with more than $112 million in art and wine, with another $40 million or more potentially coming next month. While it certainly looks like the billionaire is doing some serious housecleaning, Christie’s hasn’t offered an explanation, and Koch hasn’t publicly connected the sales to any broader plans, though in the release Koch says that he hopes “art lovers around the world can take the same enjoyment as I have, in collecting these works my hope is that collectors will find something that speaks to their passion and that they are able to share it with their friends and loved ones.”

For the upcoming sale, Koch is turning his attention to European and Latin American art. Leading the group is Monet’s Champ d’avoine et coquelicots (1890), a landscape depicting a field of oats and poppies near the artist’s home in Giverny, France. Koch bought the painting in 1985, and the work carries an estimate of $12 million to $18 million.

Sharing top billing is Cézanne’s Tasse, verre et fruits, a still life painted around 1877 that features apples, a cup, and a glass arranged on a tabletop. Koch acquired the painting in 1986, and Christie’s has given it the same $12 million to $18 million estimate. Both paintings will appear in the house’s 20th Century Evening Sale.

Another highlight is Matisse’s Jeune femme fardée à l’orientale (La bayadère), a 1929 painting of a nude inspired by the classical ballet La Bayadère. It’s expected to bring between $5 million and $7 million.

A Degas work, Scène de ballet, is estimated at $3 million to $5 million. The pastel over monotype has a particularly interesting history: it was originally purchased directly from Degas by Philadelphia collector Annie Riddle Scott on the advice of Impressionist painter Mary Cassatt. (Another impression of the underlying monotype belongs to the Clark Art Institute in Williamstown, Massachusetts.)

Koch’s collection also includes Rivera’s Vendedora de flores en Xochimilco (1929) and Miró’s Peinture (1950), each estimated at $2.5 million to $3.5 million. A 1971 Chagall painting, Danseuse à la robe fleurie, carries a $1.2 million to $1.8 million estimate, while Gabriele Münter’s Kind mit Puppe (1909) is expected to bring between $900,000 and $1.2 million.

Koch, an industrialist, America’s Cup winner, and longtime collector, has spent decades assembling collections that range from fine art to rare wines. “I feel very fortunate that with hard work, business success, and a great deal of luck, I have been able to collect things that resonate with me,” Koch said in a statement. “The masterpieces in this sale are among my favorites.”

The works will be spread across Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale, Impressionist and Modern Art Day Sale, and Works on Paper Sale during the house’s November marquee week in New York.

item.title: Friedel Dzubas Dreamed of Showing His Paintings in a Church—Now He Has His Wish - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Friedel Dzubas spent most of his career making enormous, vibrant Color Field–esque abstract paintings. But for a brief stint in the early 1960s, he abandoned color altogether. He became so taken with the outcome of that period—a series of soft yet stark black-and-white paintings—that he dreamed of finding a Baroque chapel somewhere in Europe and covering its walls with them.

He never got his chapel. But more than 30 years after his death, the German-born painter has come surprisingly close.

On opening night of “Friedel Dzubas: Darkness into Light” at Nathalie Karg Gallery in Manhattan, Robert Keith, a director at the gallery, walked me through a room filled with the artist’s rarely seen black-and-white paintings. Keith pointed out that the building was once a school belonging to the neighboring Ukrainian church. Dzubas, he said, would have been enormously proud to see his work displayed there. It was something he’d wanted all his life.

“If Dzubas sees us from above, I’m sure he’s very happy,” Karg told me a few days later during a chat on the second floor of the gallery.

The exhibition, organized with Nicolas Graille of the gallery Jules Lazare, revisits one of the strangest and most personal periods in the career of an artist who knew just about everybody in the New York art world but never became quite as famous as many of his friends.

Dzubas was born in Berlin in 1915 to a Catholic mother and a Jewish father. He fled Nazi Germany for the United States in 1939 and eventually found himself among the painters who would change American art. He knew Jackson Pollock, shared a studio with Helen Frankenthaler, and became friends with the influential critic Clement Greenberg. He participated in the famous Ninth Street Show in 1951 and had a solo exhibition at Leo Castelli’s gallery in 1958. In other words, he was hardly an outsider. He was there when Abstract Expressionism was becoming the dominant force in American painting.

Yet Dzubas could never outrun the enormous shadow of his better-known contemporaries. Yes, his pictures found their way into major museums, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Guggenheim, and he had a retrospective at the Hirshhorn Museum in Washington, D.C., in 1983. But his name doesn’t carry anything like the recognition of Pollock or Frankenthaler.

Why not? Karg thinks the answer may be as simple as changing tastes. “It’s fashion, it’s taste, it’s the generations that change,” she said. Sometimes an artist enjoys enormous success, only to fall out of favor as collectors move on. Sometimes an artist’s moment arrives much later.

Dzubas’s black paintings are a prime example of this phenomenon.

In 1959, after finally becoming an American citizen, the artist returned to Germany for the first time in 20 years. It was an emotionally complicated homecoming. In the late 1930s he escaped a country that was descending into Nazism, leaving his family behind. According to Graille, who has worked closely with the artist’s daughter and estate, surviving letters from Dzubas’s mother suggest she was deeply hurt by his departure and long absence. “You left, you abandoned us,” Graille recalled her writing in one of her letters to Dzubas.

Exactly what happened during that visit is impossible to reconstruct. Dzubas traveled through Germany and Austria, visiting Baroque churches and spending time at a monastery. The trip seems to have awakened his interest in the Catholic traditions of his childhood, along with memories of the country he’d left behind. “He was always, at his core, I think, still a traditional European painter,” Graille said.

Soon afterward, Dzubas began making paintings that looked almost nothing like the colorful abstractions associated with his name.

The bright, expansive shapes had disappeared. In their place came black marks, gray washes, looping lines, and dense arrangements of brushstrokes somewhere between Twombly’s chalk drawings and Pollock’s contained chaos. Some look almost like handwriting, though there’s nothing to read. Others suggest crosses, figures, or religious scenes. Several have borders worked into the composition that hint at the ornate frames associated with Old Master works or religious paintings, giving them the appearance of devotional objects.

The titles offer clues of what Dzubas was thinking: Temptation, Betrayal, Rex, and Walpurgis, the last a reference to a German festival with pagan roots.

The works were shown at Robert Elkon Gallery in 1962, where the critical response was mixed. In the New York Times, Brian O’Doherty wrote that the works appeared gloomy and largely unconvincing. Donald Judd, who back then was a young critic and artist, was more impressed, even if his praise was charmingly restrained. “This one is not bad,” Judd wrote, after dismissing Dzubas’s previous two exhibitions.

The paintings didn’t find much of a market, either. Dzubas soon returned to color, and the black works largely disappeared from view. Karg thinks the timing was unfortunate. By the early ’60s, the art world was falling in love with Pop art. Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein were offering collectors bright colors, recognizable images, and a decidedly different mood. Dzubas, meanwhile, was painting pictures that were, as Karg put it, “sinister.” Not exactly what collectors at the time were looking for.

Graille believes these paintings could be the most revealing works Dzubas ever made, bringing together his German upbringing, American career, religious interests, and complicated family history. “To me, this body of work is probably the most overlooked of his whole career, and the most original, most personal work that he made,” he said.

Graille first became involved with Dzubas’s work nearly a decade ago, when he met the artist’s daughter, Hani. He later began working with the estate, which had continued to find buyers for Dzubas’s better-known paintings of the ’60s and ’70s. The black works, however, had received little attention.

When Graille and Karg met through a mutual friend, they realized their interests complemented one another. Karg had been increasingly interested in revisiting historical artists, while Graille was working with estates and establishing his own gallery, Jules Lazare, which he named in tribute to his late mother.

The two remain separate businesses but share some expenses and collaborate on exhibitions. Next month they’ll open a show of work by Larry Poons. For Karg, the partnership provides an opportunity to look beyond the younger artists who dominate so much of the contemporary gallery business.

“There are so many good artists, but they have never been really accounted for,” she said.

And collectors are beginning to pay attention to Dzubas again. According to data from ARTDAI, the artist’s annual auction sales have grown considerably over the past decade, from $468,226 across 14 lots offered in 2016 to more than $1.6 million across 25 lots offered in 2025. In May, his painting Entrance, offered alongside another work, sold at Christie’s for $160,000, against a high estimate of $100,000. (All figures are hammer prices.)

The market hasn’t been entirely immune to the broader slowdown. Dzubas’s sell-through rate has slipped to 81.3 percent so far in 2026, with 3 of 16 lots failing to find buyers.

Still, when I asked Graille about the market, he seemed almost offended by the premise. “The market is great, but who cares?” he said. “Art is about more than sales.” He’s also encouraged by renewed institutional interest. Graille said that German collector Reinhard Ernst, whose museum in Wiesbaden holds a major collection of Frankenthaler’s work, has been assembling what he described as the world’s largest collection of Dzubas paintings. Ernst now owns 12 works from the black series, some of which are on loan to the New York exhibition. The museum is planning a Dzubas retrospective for June 2027.

The New York show has found buyers, too. Karg said several paintings had sold, with others on reserve. Graille described the exhibition as nearly sold out, with particular interest in the larger works. For paintings that struggled to find buyers in 1962, that’s quite a turnaround.

But the more interesting question may be what this renewed attention means for Dzubas’s reputation. His colorful paintings have for years secured his place in the history of postwar American abstraction. The black series suggests there’s another, more complicated story to tell. And that brings the artist back to the church.

In a 1982 interview, Dzubas described becoming obsessed with the possibility of filling a chapel with his black drawings. He imagined them covering the architecture, turning the space into something between an exhibition and a religious experience. He died in 1994, never having realized the project.

Now, in a former church school on Manhattan’s Lower East Side, some of those paintings have finally found a home that would have made sense to him. It isn’t the Baroque chapel he imagined, but it’s probably the next best thing.

item.title: Paul Pfeiffer on the Spectacle of Politics - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — In the early 1990s, Paul Pfeiffer began producing a series of striking interventions in found video footage, often featuring celebrated sports figures, to highlight the effects of media and fame on not just individuals but also the larger body politic. Using innovative post-production techniques, he removed key elements from scenes of professional boxers and basketball players, isolating them in various arenas, teasing out the uncanny undercurrents in such late modern spectacles. 

Pfeiffer’s work further heightened the stakes of these scenes of pop culture by invoking art historical figures from classical sources, including caryatids from his eponymous 2003–4 series, and modern painting, as seen in his 1999 digital video installation “Fragment of a Crucifixion (after Francis Bacon).” He has also developed a wide-ranging practice of drawing and sculpture, as seen in his series of sculptural maquettes and imagined plans for a million-seat stadium, all named some version of Vitruvian Figure, and woodcarvings of pop singer Justin Bieber in the style of Jesus on the Cross — “Justin Bieber Legs Crucified (Seville)” from 2026 — which feature in his current exhibition at Galerie Perrotin in Los Angeles.

Hyperallergic: What do you think about the scaling up of mass culture in recent generations, and how it creates collective affects that can be appealing, but also lead to dystopian outcomes? I’m thinking of the quote, “A million Elvis fans can't be wrong” — would a billion Swifties gathering be a stadium too far? 

Paul Pfeiffer: There's a proliferation of stadiums, often connected to cyclical events like the World Cup or the Olympics, traveling from city to city, such that the architecture mirrors this kind of rhythm.

If we think about soft power and the amount of politics conducted through the World Cup, and the listlessness and questionable effectiveness of the United Nations now, perhaps the stadium is actually the replacement for the UN as a symbolic gathering point to conduct world politics. It certainly hides as much as it reveals, but has become a staging ground for political pronouncements. In that way it’s beyond symbolic — the athletes' bodies move beyond the agonistic encounters in the stadium.

H: I think about Iranian athletes who trained outside the United States border during the World Cup due to the US government’s unwillingness to host them overnight, and faced this greater adversity just getting to their jobs. I think also of those people marching out of the UN assembly during Netanyahu’s speech, who voted with their bodies. 

PP: For me, it's the play of the visible and the invisible, or the facade and the informal production scheme behind the facade. This is present in the ways politics are conducted through culture now, a formal symbolic aspect that carries a certain kind of weight. I agree about the spectacle of so many delegates walking out on Netanyahu is heartening — a bit of agency when we needed it.

item.title: Nathan Fielder Is a Performance Artist in Disguise - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Editor’s Note: This review contains spoilers.

As an art historian, it's hard not to relate what you see in everyday life to history — not in the sense that every lily pad recalls Monet or snowballs bring David Hammons to mind, but in the sense that sometimes art really does imitate life. This happened to me recently, maybe 10 minutes into Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything. I watched Fielder hold painful, prolonged eye contact with Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted fraudster whose eerily large blue eyes seem to enact their own kind of performance. Naturally, I thought of Marina Abramović’s “The Artist is Present” (2010). Perhaps it’s an obvious, pretentious comparison. But hear me out: Is Fielder a documentarian, or is he a performance artist playing one? 

Artist Martha Wilson recently defined performance art as an intervention that unfolds in real time, often placing the artist’s body at the center of the action. The genre has long tested the limits of what an artist’s body can do, and what an audience will tolerate: Chris Burden had himself shot with a .22-caliber gun in “Shoot” (1971); Yoko Ono invited audience members to cut away her clothing in “Cut Piece” (1964); and Carolee Schneemann pulled a scroll from her vagina in “Interior Scroll” (1975). These works differ considerably, but each makes the artist’s actions and the responses they provoke central to the work. 

Fielder, too, puts himself in the middle of things. In You Can See Everything, he spends 34 days filming and questioning Holmes, her partner Billy Evans, and their two children. Eventually, he moves into the guesthouse of their California beachfront rental, just before Holmes begins her 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors and patients of Theranos, whose blood-testing technology falsely claimed it could run a wide range of tests on a few drops of blood. The couple frames their participation as an act of “radical transparency,” hoping to persuade the public that Holmes is innocent. They chose Fielder as their documentarian, they explain, because he “thinks outside the box” just like they do. Game recognizes game.

Fielder’s move turns observation into participation. His proximity to the family becomes part of the experiment, shaping the behavior he records. In one scene, he films himself lurking at a distance as Billy and Holmes embrace. In another, he sits close to Holmes on a couch; a hand strokes her shoulder, and for a moment it seems to belong to Fielder, until the camera reveals Billy on the other side. But the film invites us to imagine a silent intimacy growing between Holmes and Fielder that it never confirms. Elsewhere, Holmes texts flirtatiously, “fyi you can totally see everything.” The title begins to feel less like a promise of transparency and more like provocation: Who is watching who? What does each person want seen?

item.title: ‘Desiring Machines’ Dares Us to Imagine a Healthy Relationship with Technology - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot, a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet. The column will appear every other Monday.

A classic illustration of a world that has fallen to technology first appeared on Facebook in the 2010s and has been circulating online ever since. You likely know it: Rows of bent heads gazing at their phone screens; each face replaced by a ray of light sucked towards the screen. By 2026, the illustration has become boomer meme par excellence, but it captures the familiar feeling that our relationship with technology is one-sided, hypnotic, and vampiric. AI-induced existential panic has only heightened this feeling, leading to a keen desire to set some boundaries with our devices.

Cue the Instagram infographics on how to develop analog hobbies; viral videos of young people simply socializing without their phones, digital detox camps, and the under 13 social media bans. Cue the paranoia that every so-called analog activity is inherently performative, such as reading in public.
But what if these measures were misguided? What if instead of punishing ourselves for our technological entanglements, we got curious?

That’s the question at the center of “Desiring Machines” a new exhibition on view at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Mar del Plata, Argentina. At a time when it seems that the future can be clearly read in the inevitable march of technological advancement, curator Augustina Rinaldi leans on the work of philosophers’ Gilles Deleuze and Felix Guattari to make an alternative claim: it is not innovation but desire which shapes social transformation, and thus, it is only by understanding our desires that we might generate new and unexpected futures.

The exhibition feature ten Argentine artists and is on view until November 2. Upon entering, one has the feeling of having entered into a laboratory. Organic and inorganic materials mingle in a controlled, sterile environment pregnant with possibility and invention. Device for Exhaling the Tremor (2025), a large sculpture by Celeste Martinez Abburra, explicitly recalls the stainless steel and glass beakers of a chemistry laboratory. Delicate glass vessels suspended by metal and connected by pipes gather condensation that drips into a pool of fetid water. In Joaquin Fargas’s Biosphere Project (2006-2026), aquatic plants floating in sealed globes are installed on a tripod of spidery, chrome pincers.

Two video works elsewhere reflect the uncanny, cold environment Rinaldi has curated in an attempt to capture, “an intermediate horizon” between the present and the future, as as per the wall text.

You Will Become Salt (2024) by Indira Montoya is set in the state of Córdoba hundreds of years after its inundation in a series of floods. Using photogammetry, a technique which renders 2D surfaces into 3D models, and game engines, Montoya directs a virtual drone that hovers over the ruins of cities and its strange, frozen residents. Celeste Martínez Aburrá’s film Cartography of the Infra-Thin (2025), also set in Córdoba, features a white field covered in snow where the artist has installed a series of smoke machines. The camera flies through this bizarre set of ice and vapor.

Facing this is Miguel Harte’s “Danza” series (2025), consisting of a ghostly forest of tree stumps bursting with oily, metallic forms; or alien vines invading their crevices. It’s an uncomfortable image: what is whole and organic has been penetrated by the technological tentacle, mirroring our own hopelessly enmeshed relationship with our devices and the infrastructures of power which produce them.

The work of Deleuze and Guattari provides a useful context to understand these penetrative sculptures that sit on a discomfiting spectrum of organism and machine. The title of the exhibition is borrowed from their 1972 book “Anti-Oedipus: Capitalism and Schizophrenia” in which they mount an attack on both Freud’s psychoanalytic theory that desire stems from absence, and his related “Oedipus complex” which proposes that the unconscious is structured by an incestuous romantic rivalry—or as Deleuze and Guattari put it, the “daddy-mommy-me” trinity. Their understanding of desire is that it is not produced by lack but through any form of relation, including one’s relation to objects. The authors propose a more systemic understanding of desire as one cog in an organic machine, infinitely reacting to other machines.

Consider Martina Servio Olavide’s sculptural installation Untitled (2025). The work consists of a transparent female figure, sculpted with her back arched in a bridge position and filled halfway with water. She has no arms, and is surrounded by small, round mirrors. Her mannequin head is serene, but a set of external ribs peek out from underneath like the bony grip of a witch. The living element in the objectified shell, the splayed offering before a set of mirrors which both reflect her and the audience.

One reading of Untitled is as a diagram of how desire shapes our perception of one another and of ourselves. Even more, how that gaze is projected online.

The work doesn’t condemn social media, but rather withholds the predictable interpretation (it’s all objectification!), forcing viewers in for a closer look. Whether it’s the “Danza” series or the Biospheres Project, the works on view push us to consider that a flat rejection of technology is an overly simplistic reaction. If we confront the desire perpetuating these terrifying enmeshments, we might become capable of imagining a more creative future for these relationships.

In other words, desire, in an unrepressed form, explodes the channels through which it is expected to flow. Here, art works to excite a deeper perception of where our desire is being frustrated or forcibly channeled, and where it might flow if the dam broke. What might emerge if that desire was unleashed? “Desiring Machines” is not a diorama of the future. It is a snapshot of a process perpetually in motion. Our dance with objects, and through those objects, how we dance with each other.

item.title: Dreamy Digital Illustrations by Rebecca Zwanzig Tap into Art History and Nostalgia - Colossal
item.description:
From the atmospheric tones of the Pacific Northwest to Victorian-era textile patterns to antique dishware designs, Rebecca Zwanzig—the artist behind High West Wild—draws on a wide range of influences. “I grew up in the bluegrass state of Kentucky, and some of my earliest visual memories come from going to auctions and estate sales with my grandma in rural Kentucky,” the artist tells Colossal. “I was always drawn to the patterns on old plates, the embroidery on tablecloths, vintage textiles, and all of these little objects and keepsakes that had clearly belonged to someone and had a life before they ended up there.”

Currently based in Portland, Oregon, by way of Washington’s mountains and Nevada’s desert, the artist draws on this nostalgia in her digital works. Reminiscent of late 19th and early 20th-century motifs, her botanicals emerge from associations with landscapes she has lived in and influences from the not-so-distant past.

“I’ve always loved vintage textiles and illustration, scientific botanical art, folk art, and the groovy typography and design from the ’60s and ’70s,” Zwanzig says. “My colors tend to come from that same place, too. Lots of earthy 1970s tones…I love anything dark and moody, but I also love really bright, saturated color, so I tend to move between the two.”

Zwanzig’s illustrations often incorporate symmetry and the satisfying repetition of patterns, evoking Art Nouveau and the Arts and Crafts Movement exemplified by the likes of William Morris. Portraits of insects, crystals, and shells, and other natural phenomena also bring to mind natural history tomes such as Lorenz Oken’s Allgemaine Naturgeschichte Für Alle Stände or The Hudson Transparencies.

Her practice developed around early interests in graphic design and oil painting, which she still turns to occasionally to explore the texture of the analog medium. Even her digital pieces created in Procreate or Adobe Illustrator are derived from sketches she first makes by hand to compose lush gradients we associate with oil.

Clients including Starbucks, Marine Layer, Anna Sui, Free People, and more have licensed Zwanzig’s work, and she’s currently in the midst of a personal project of designing a complete tarot deck. If you’re in Seattle next month, you can see Zwanzig’s work at the Renegade Craft Fair, which runs from November 20 to 22. Follow updates and see more from her on the High West Wild Instagram.

item.title: John Dilg’s Down-to-Earth Reverence - Hyperallergic
item.description:
John Dilg’s paintings don’t seem to have undergone any seismic changes during the decade I’ve been following his work, so I wasn’t sure there was anything else I could say about it. But after visiting a recent exhibition at Peter Freeman Gallery and reflecting on my experience, I realized I was wrong.  

The show included 13 paintings, 10 of which were made this year. Twelve measured 14 x 18 1/8 inches (~35.6 x 46 cm) and were oriented horizontally or vertically. The circumscribed palette of pale blues, celadon greens, browns, and off-white was present in every work, and the application was unvaried; the nub of the canvas was visible through the thin layer of paint. In addition to oil paint, Dilg used charcoal and graphite to draw the contour of his unmistakable natural forms. Except for “Wild Life” (2024), the subject of each painting is a spare, serene landscape with almost no signs of human life, often under a full moon blanketing the world in perpetual twilight. For the sameness in size, palette, and application, Dilg did not repeat himself.

item.title: Scott Kahn Invokes Dreams and Liminality in Atmospheric Landscape Paintings - Colossal
item.description:
Until a few years ago, painter Scott Kahn was living in his cousin’s attic, with a studio filled with work that he hadn’t had a lot of luck selling. Then, he began a chance correspondence with the late Canadian artist Matthew Wong, who related to Kahn’s own self-taught background and interest in magical realism. “Matthew was really a great champion of my work,” Kahn told Artnet News. “The only way I can explain it is that we were soulmates.” When Wong’s career took off in 2018, Kahn’s atmospheric, often surreal landscapes also found their audience.

Mostly working in oil on linen, Kahn creates scenes that glow beneath the bright moon or complement architectural elements seen through vignettes of trees and clouds. The works shown here were recently on view in the artist’s sweeping solo exhibition, Silent Night at David Zwirner.

We encounter nods to American regionalism, such as in “Berkshire Nightscape II” with its pronounced resemblance to Grant Wood’s bulbous, cultivated hills of rural Iowa. Other works invoke the realm of the unconscious, such “The Basement Window,” which recalls a recurring dream the artist has of his childhood home. Trees appear both inside and outside, blurring the boundary between architectural space and nature. In “The Stoop,” a mysterious, deep-forest darkness infringes upon the sunniness of front steps.

In “The Basement,” there is also a subtle connection to the interiority of the body in the trees’ vein-like branches and roots. Through structural apertures, such as a window or a balcony—including the paintings’ inherent frames—the surrounding environment is open to us but always limited. There is always a compelling edge, horizon, shadow, or disappearing path that prompts us to question whether we can truly comprehend what we see.

Kahn’s compositions often feel familiar, yet through deep contrasts, long shadows, nighttime scenes, and portal-like framing, he invokes a sense of enigma and liminality. The scenes are often stretched, as if seen through a wide-angle lens, and there is an indelible sense of transition, whether from night to day, sleeping to waking, or imagination to reality. “I don’t get too bogged down in what a landscape actually is,” Kahn says. “It’s more a vehicle to express a mood. That, to me, is the value of a landscape.”

See more on the artist’s Instagram.

item.title: Wish You Were Here! Rose Sanderson’s Witty Postcards Conjure a Strange Reality - Colossal
item.description:
Like many artists, Rose Sanderson began a body of work during the early days of the pandemic as a sort of balm for the harsh realities of the world. “I started playing with escapism and imagination, mixing reality and fiction, and the blurring of childhood memories and nostalgia,” she says of her surreal paintings on vintage postcards. “Many of the images are in seaside towns, influenced by growing up in one myself through the ’80s and ’90s.”

Playing with scale, Sanderson renders scenes that evoke the Creature Features of early cinema: an enormous crab is on the verge of scuttling over a beach filled with people, a tiger lounges alongside an unsuspecting man, and a zig-zagged fissure bisects the ground around an amusement park. But thanks to the artist’s wit, the paintings are more humorous than horrifying, plunging viewers into a bizarre dreamland where the uncanny is always lurking around the corner.

Sanderson has been collecting the postcards from thrift stores, antique shops, markets, and online retailers for several years, which she’s added to a collection started by her grandparents. “There is something special about these snippets of history that give me a warm fuzzy feeling, and I love a lot of the aged, saturated colours, too.”

Having reached 50 paintings, Sanderson’s series will be on view from November 11 to December 23 at Aberystwyth Arts Centre. A limited-edition book featuring all of the works will be available as well. Follow along for updates on the artist’s Instagram.

item.title: An Abbey in France Discovered Previously Unknown Wall Sketches by Odilon Redon - ARTnews.com
item.description:
For more than a century, a suite of murals by Symbolist painter Odilon Redon have decorated the library of the Abbaye de Fontfroide, an 11th-century former monastery in the South of France. When they were removed earlier this year for the first time since their installation to be loaned for a high-profile exhibition, a set of test drawings, until then unknown, by Redon were uncovered.

“It was a great surprise—nobody imagined the existence of these sketches,” Alexandre d’Andoque de Sériège, Abbaye de Fontfroide’s director, told ARTnews in an interview. “It amuses just to imagine Redon painting them on the wall.”

Installed upon their completion in 1911, the three paneled works—La Jour (Day), La Nuit (Night), and Le Silence (Silence)—were commissioned by Gustave Fayet. Fayet was one of the turn of century’s great French collectors, but he is now little-known. The breadth of Fayet’s holdings is now coming into view via a blockbuster exhibition, “Gustave Fayet, Collector-Designer: Icons of Modern Art,” at the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris, which has gathered around 250 works of the 750 works that once passed through his hands.

The drawings’ discovery was even more surprising because neither Fayet nor Redon had ever written about their existence, either in correspondence to each other or to other members of the French avant-garde. It’s possible that they might have been an initial test for a fresco, but “a fresco in the library would have required Redon to stay very long in Fontfroide. It’s also physically a very hard job,” d’Andoque de Sériège, who is also Fayet’s grandson, said. “So, I think it’s really just a painting for fun.”

That theory is supported by the fact that the newly discovered wall drawings don’t resemble the final works, which were begun in Redon’s Paris studio. “The figures are more colorful [on the wall] than the figures in panels. The shape is typical Redon, but not the choice of colors,” d’Andoque de Sériège said. “The two female figures—Madeleine and Simone [his wife and daughter]—are very tall, very important in the panels, but in the sketches on the walls they are rather small, only 30–35 centimeters high.”

Fayet met Redon in 1900 and purchased his first work by the artist the following year; he eventually came to own some 300 works of his. Fayet would visit Redon each time he took the train up to Paris, and they grew closer still when the collector’s family moved to Paris in 1905. The friendship also influenced Fayet as a painter: He started out making Realist pictures in the style of the Barbizon School before taking up the Impressionist style. When he met Redon, Fayet “moved to a sort of emotional painting, and I think that’s why he bought so many paintings from Redon and the Nabis,” d’Andoque de Sériège said.

Fayet’s purchase of Fontfroide slowed down his collecting, which began in 1899, the year he took over the family business and purchased 41 works from the collection of Armand Carbol, another winemaker from Béziers. His decision to buy the abbey was one that came of familiarity. The Domaine de Vedilhan, one of the Fayet’s family vineyards near Narbonne, is about 12 miles northeast of the Abbaye de Fontfroide.

“Fayet’s family knew Fontfroide for a long time before Fayet himself bought it in 1908,” d’Andoque de Sériège said. “His father, Gabriel, was a painter [who] painted the cloister of Fontfroide and the portrait of the last abbot of Fontfroide,” whom the Fayet visited in 1895 with Madeline.

But Fayet also wanted to prevent Fontfroide’s destruction. After the 1901 Law of Associations, which suppressed religious orders and seized their properties, many historical religious sites were bought so their masonry could be repurposed to make new buildings, according to d’Andoque de Sériège. (Fayet was first outbid in his quest to buy Fontfroide, which had already been sold twice, but he offered 10 percent more, triggering an auction, where he paid 49,925 francs to buy it in January 1908.)

“[Fayet] intended to turn his property into a vibrant, creative place, imbued with a fully Symbolist philosophy in which great pagan myths could enter into dialogue with Christian sensibilities in a natural setting steeped in a sacred tradition,” d’Andoque de Sériège writes in an essay he coauthored with art historian Pierre Pinchon on Redon’s decoration for Fontfroide. “Fayet’s intentions naturally appealed to Redon, who had recently been steering his work toward a pantheistic celebration of nature and a glorification of the solar myths through Apollonian, Orphic, and floral subjects.”

Redon first visited Fontfroide in October 1908, and when he arrived, he immediately noticed the statue of Diana and Apollo that Fayet had installed near the entrance. That would ultimately impact the design for La Jour. When Redon returned in March 1910 for a 10-day stay, the restoration of the library had been completed, and he had a better sense of how his commission would sit in the space.

“At that period, they discussed the project because it was easier to see room, the importance of the wall, to look at the light through the windows,” d’Andoque de Sériège said. “We guess—we are 99 percent sure—that it is during that that stay that Redon made the sketches we discovered when we removed the panels.”

While Redon made decorative panels for other sites in France, the panels at Fontfroide are the only ones that still remain in situ in their original location, according to d’Andoque de Sériège. As their titles indicate, the two larger works, Le Jour and Le Nuit, are in dialogue with each other.

“The two decorative panels are a testament to the whole career of Redon,” he said. “La Nuit is an echo of the ‘Noirs’ period of Redon, and Le Jour echoes the second period of Redon, with the theme of Apollo and Diana, but more generally with all the flowers, the bouquets, and the use of color.”

He continued, “The second reason for the importance of this decoration is it reflects finally the taste of Gustave Fayet, who first collected the ‘Noirs’ and then moved to the flowers and mythological themes of Redon. Fayet also sold [parts of his collection] in 1910, just a few months before, so it’s a period where he is reorganizing his collection around Gauguin, van Gogh, Redon, and others.”

After the Fondation Louis Vuitton exhibition, the Redon works will return to Fontfroide, as their installation was classified a few years ago by the French state as a historical monument, joining the cloister, abbey, and chapter house which were designated as such in the 19th century. Fontfroide had to receive a special authorization from the Ministry of Culture in order to loan them to the exhibition.

“It is the first and only time we will do that,” d’Andoque de Sériège said. “Very few people have heard of Fayet. The exhibition at Fondation Louis Vuittion will shed light on Fayet, but it will be visible only during five months in Paris. After the exhibition, the only thing you can see from Fayet is Fontfroide, and what he did for the restoration: the sculpture, the gardens, the tiles, the library, everything. We have to be much more precise and say much more about Fayet at Fontfroide because today when you visit Fontfroide, we say very little about Fayet, which was a mistake from my family.”

item.title: From Paris, In Solidarity - Hyperallergic
item.description:
When journalist Naima Morelli arrived in Paris last weekend, she could smell the scent of burning plastic in the air. Thus began her quest to report on the city’s surreal week of exhibitions and blue-chip art fairs, with million-dollar artworks changing hands as students protest deteriorating education and public service systems. Morelli captures the atmosphere, both dystopian and hopeful, in her dispatch below.

In another city with a rich history of protest, New York performance artist Martha Wilson reviews a history of the Culture Wars told in Isaac Butler’s new book The Perfect Moment, reflecting on the work of the NEA Four, David Wojnarowicz, and other artists who defended creative expression in a time not unlike our own. Also today, Duaa Shah takes a deep-dive into the way art circulates in the legal system as both treatment and evidence, particularly for displaced communities seeking justice.

More, as always, including a review of the Toronto Biennial and the unlikely star of a new Jean-Michel Basquiat biopic: Kid Cudi.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

Portrait of a Paris Art Week on Fire

“The people in the art world are courageous,” a collector told me at Asia Now, the first of the Paris art fairs that opened early in the week on Monday, in the heat of the protests. “But I would still like to be back at my hotel before 7pm, you know, just in case.”

Anyone who is a regular at Paris Art Week has a collection of stories about something going wrong. In 2022, there were strikes and cost-of-living marches. In October 2023, France was on high terror alert, and one of the bomb threats that emptied the airports of the country’s major cities led to, among other things, my plane landing in the middle of the French countryside. A couple of trains later, and voilà: I was in Paris in time for the vernissages. | Naima Morelli

Read More

How Art Can Deliver Justice for Refugees

In the legal system, art created by refugees and incarcerated people can serve both as a form of therapy and as evidence of mass atrocities. | Duaa Shah
